## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why can a robot pass every trial and still lack the evidence needed for deployment?_

A robot that repeatedly opens one door has supplied evidence about that door, its own hardware, and the conditions of those trials. It has not established how it will behave at a displaced latch, with a different payload, or after its sensors drift, and a flawless record from a short campaign remains consistent with a policy that fails a substantial fraction of its attempts. Its admitted actions also change the observations it receives, so agreement with recorded demonstrations cannot substitute for testing the resulting motion. Physical trials expose that feedback, but each consumes time and mechanical life, every further factor of ten in demonstrated reliability costs roughly ten times the trials, and protective interventions stop some trajectories before their consequences unfold. A team that reads a clean record as readiness releases the machine into conditions no trial visited and credits the learned policy with protection its supervisors supplied. Evaluation exists to prevent that error. It ties each task outcome to the conditions sampled, keeps every intervention in the record, states the uncertainty that remains, and names the uncovered conditions the rest of the machine must guard. Because actions cross an irreversible causal boundary, evidence of policy competence must remain distinct from permission to move.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Interpret physical success rates as conditional evidence about a specified machine, environment, and trial protocol
- Interpret completion and intervention metrics without crediting the policy for protection supplied by its supervision
- Compare open-loop prediction accuracy with closed-loop behavior shaped by the policy's own actions
- Select the evidence regime (replay, simulation, shadow operation, or constrained physical testing) that can answer a given evaluation question
- Design a predeclared trial protocol with fixed outcome rules and full-denominator accounting of interventions and aborts
- Calculate confidence bounds, trial counts, and test time for a zero-failure campaign under stated sampling assumptions
- Construct an evaluation record that bounds its operational claim and identifies coverage gaps and required protections
- Evaluate which rare failures remain unsupported by feasible testing and the available statistical assumptions
- Diagnose how hardware differences, environmental changes, and stopping rules alter the claim a campaign can support

:::
## From Clean Runs to Bounded Claims {#sec-evaluation-door-campaign}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-door-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DOOR CAMPAIGN ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: chapter opener, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the lease fallacy.
# │ Show: the evaluated campaign (latch task, base stopped) and the machine
# │       values the chapter quotes: approach speed, tripwire, latch limit, rack
# │       capacity, chunk inference target, chunk period, and chunk lease;
# │       plus the Part II funnel
# │       the completed record carries (ledger cells, supported cells,
# │       known absences, manifest omissions).
# │ How: registry fields of the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle;
# │      the standoff and the ledger counts (from @sec-data and
# │      @sec-training) are chapter-local inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_frequency, check, MarkdownStr

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EvalMachine:
    """The latch campaign Ch7 evaluates, on the book's running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    standoff = 2.0 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; base start distance from the door
    v_approach = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative; guarded approach, the declared ODD's speed
    f_latch_limit = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative; latch damage limit
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative; contact tripwire that ends an attempt (@sec-data)
    rack_capacity = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen; tote-rack capacity
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk policy rate
    t_chunk_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 of the ACT chunk policy incl. vision (M5)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen; chunk lease
    n_plate_positions = 3  # category: illustrative; nominal and two displaced plates, the scenario ledger of @sec-data
    ledger_speeds = [AISLE.v_latch_approach, AISLE.v_latch_high]  # category: illustrative; the ledger's two approach speeds
    n_supported = 1  # category: illustrative; the nominal plate at the guarded approach (LatchScenarioLedger in @sec-data)
    n_omissions = 2  # category: illustrative; soft penalty contact and missing transport lag, the manifest's omission log

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    n_speeds = len(ledger_speeds)
    n_cells = n_plate_positions * n_speeds
    n_absences = n_cells - n_supported

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_approach.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded approach is not 0.03 m/s")
    check(abs(f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit is not 100 N")
    check(abs(f_trip.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Contact tripwire is not 15 N")
    check(f_trip < f_latch_limit, "The tripwire must end an attempt well below the damage limit")
    check(abs(rack_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is not 50 kg")
    check(abs(chunk_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk period is not 50 ms")
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease is not 60 ms")
    check(chunk_period < t_lease, "Chunk period must fit inside the lease")
    check(abs(t_chunk_infer.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk inference target is not 40 ms")
    check(t_chunk_infer < chunk_period, "Chunk inference must finish within the chunk period")
    check(n_cells == 6 and n_supported == 1 and n_absences == 5, "Ledger should have one supported cell of six (matches @sec-data)")
    check(n_omissions == 2, "Manifest omission log holds two unclosed departures (matches @sec-training)")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    standoff_str = fmt_length(standoff, precision=0)
    v_approach_str = fmt_velocity(v_approach, precision=2)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    rack_capacity_str = fmt_mass(rack_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period)
    t_chunk_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_infer)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease)
    _words = {1: "one", 2: "two", 3: "three", 5: "five", 6: "six"}
    n_plate_positions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_plate_positions])
    n_speeds_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_speeds])
    n_cells_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_cells])
    n_supported_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_supported])
    n_absences_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_absences])
    n_omissions_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_omissions])
```

The checkpoint `latch-bc-01` arrives from offline imitation learning with a policy manifest that declares exactly one supported condition, the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach. The manifest marks where the policy's training evidence ends, and evaluation asks what physical trials can establish inside that line. The recovery candidate `latch-bc-recovery-02`, whose wider claim new experience still has to earn, receives its own campaign later in the chapter (@sec-evaluation-recovery-update). `latch-bc-01` is flashed onto the warehouse mobile manipulator for a nominal validation campaign. In each trial, the mobile base begins `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide) from the spring-latched cage door, drives forward, and comes to a complete halt. With the base at rest, the manipulator executes a guarded approach at `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str`, unlatches the mechanism, and opens the door without crossing the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire or drawing a human intervention. Suppose the robot completes twenty consecutive runs this way, an empirical success rate of $\ObservedSuccessFraction = 1.00$ (100 percent). On a static vision or language benchmark, an unblemished score might suggest that the model is ready for production. On physical hardware, twenty clean runs leave the deployment decision open. They establish only a wide lower confidence bound, one that a policy failing a substantial fraction of its attempts can still satisfy, and they reveal nothing about failure modes too rare to appear in twenty draws.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The policy manifest, which records how a checkpoint was produced and the operating domain it declares, is established in @sec-training-policy-manifest.
:::

The gap between that perfect score and a deployable claim comes from three ways in which physical evaluation departs from the static protocol of machine learning, where engineers draw a held-out dataset once from a stationary distribution, score each example independently, and treat the aggregate as a faithful descriptor of model quality. First, a physical policy selects its own test distribution. Every admitted action alters the environment and determines the observations that follow, so no pre-recorded dataset can stand in for the states the policy will visit. This is the second law, endogenous data (principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}), acting on evaluation. The same feedback that pushes a cloned policy off its demonstrations also decides which states a test campaign samples. Second, every trial consumes test-cell time, battery charge, and mechanical life, which keeps sample counts small and each sample expensive. Third, a physical trial delivers kinetic energy across the causal boundary, and that energy cannot be recalled. When an interlock, a contact tripwire, or a safety operator aborts an errant motion before damage occurs, the trial ends early and leaves a censored observation that is neither an unequivocal success nor an unmitigated crash. Aerospace, automotive, and industrial automation engineers combine physical tests with model-based arguments about controller stability and protection. The learned proposer in this campaign arrives without such a certificate, so its task reliability must be bounded by finite empirical sampling under the declared conditions.

Closed-loop evaluation therefore asks what a finite campaign of physical trials can establish about a learned proposer, and what it must leave for the rest of the machine to handle. Four obligations answer that question, and they order this chapter. A success rate is meaningful only when bound to a declared population of hardware states, environmental conditions, and trial procedures, with every protective intervention kept out of the policy's credit (@sec-evaluation-what-measured). The evidence must come from a regime that can expose the failure in question, which for most physical failures means routing proposals through the real permission path rather than scoring them against logs (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics and @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes). A finite record becomes a defensible bound only under a protocol fixed before the first run, and each additional "nine" of demonstrated reliability costs roughly ten times the trials (@sec-evaluation-trial-protocol through @sec-evaluation-trial-limits). Finally, the evaluation record, the link in the record chain after the policy manifest, must state which conditions were tested and which were not, and it must turn every untested condition, together with every hazard too rare for any campaign to sample, into an obligation for the runtime permission path (@sec-evaluation-logs and @sec-evaluation-limits).

The first obligation begins with the twenty runs themselves. Before that perfect fraction can mean anything, the campaign must fix its outcome rules, define the operational population it sampled, and separate what the policy achieved from what supervision supplied. A defensible evaluation record never credits the learned proposer with successes that hardware interlocks or supervisory overrides actually purchased.

## Metric Coverage and Limitations of Scalar Success Rates {#sec-evaluation-what-measured}

A latch-manipulation policy that reliably opens a door during morning bench tests can jam repeatedly when confronted with a strike plate displaced by only three millimeters. Its measured success rate does not belong to the neural network weights in isolation; it characterizes the coupled dynamical system formed by the policy, the mechanical plant, the onboard compute platform, the physical environment, and the trial protocol itself. While a reproducible offline benchmark score indicates how well a model fits a frozen dataset, a physical success rate measures how the embodied closed-loop system behaves across a distribution of physical executions.

Evaluating a policy requires executing a sequence of discrete physical runs. A single trial is fully determined only when every physical parameter capable of altering the state trajectory is either explicitly controlled or systematically sampled. Formally, a single trial condition is the tuple $\TrialCondition = (\MechanicalPlantState_0, \EnvironmentParameters, \PlantParameters, \pi_\ModelParameters, \TerminationProtocol)$, drawn from an operational testing distribution $\OperationalTestDistribution$:

- The initial state vector $\MechanicalPlantState_0$ specifies the machine's starting condition, including its spatial pose (position and orientation), linear and angular velocities, and joint encoder positions.
- The environment vector $\EnvironmentParameters$ captures external physical variables, such as the tire-floor friction coefficient ($\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$), ambient illuminance, obstacle geometry, and ambient air temperature.
- The machine state $\PlantParameters$ captures physical and hardware properties sampled from the fleet manufacturing and wear distribution $\FleetManufacturingDistribution$. This encompasses unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances, battery state of charge, payload mass, tire wear, lost motion and compliance in the arm's transmissions\index{Mechanical backlash}, and sensor calibration matrices.
- The computational configuration $\pi_\ModelParameters$ represents the frozen policy weights $\ModelParameters$, numerical quantization formats (such as FP16 or INT8), real-time thread scheduling deadlines, and software driver versions.
- The termination protocol $\TerminationProtocol = (\CompletionDeadline, \GoalSet, \EvaluationPredicate)$ defines the execution deadline $\CompletionDeadline$, the spatial goal region $\GoalSet$, and the binary evaluation predicate $\EvaluationPredicate$ that maps the realized trajectory to a terminal outcome $\TrialCompletionIndicator \in \{0, 1\}$.

In static machine learning benchmarks, inputs $(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i)$ are sampled independently from a static data distribution $\StaticDataDistribution(\ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$. In Physical AI, the continuous trajectory $\text{Traj}(\TrialCondition) = (\MechanicalPlantState_0, \AdmittedControlCommand_0, \MechanicalPlantState_1, \AdmittedControlCommand_1, \dots, \MechanicalPlantState_\RolloutHorizon)$ is generated sequentially by the closed-loop physical state transition kernel:
$$\MechanicalPlantState_{t+1} \sim \PlantTransitionKernel(\MechanicalPlantState_t, \AdmittedControlCommand_t; \PlantParameters, \EnvironmentParameters), \quad \CognitivePolicyAction_{t} = \pi_\ModelParameters(\MechanicalPlantState_t), \quad \AdmittedControlCommand_t = \text{Gate}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t}, \MechanicalPlantState_t)$$
Here $\text{Gate}$ stands for the permission path, which admits, clips, or replaces each proposal $\CognitivePolicyAction_{t}$ before it becomes the applied command $\AdmittedControlCommand_t$. Its permission and controller parameters remain fixed and are archived with the evaluated configuration; changing them changes the evaluated closed loop. The true success probability under this evaluation protocol is the expected value of the binary task outcome averaged over the joint distribution of trial conditions:
$$\TrialSuccessProbability(\OperationalTestDistribution) = \mathbb{E}_{\TrialCondition \sim \OperationalTestDistribution}[\EvaluationPredicate(\text{Traj}(\TrialCondition))]$$ {#eq-eval-estimand}
where $\text{Traj}(\TrialCondition)$ is the physical trajectory generated under condition $\TrialCondition$. Altering floor friction, ambient temperature, or battery voltage modifies the physical transition kernel $\PlantTransitionKernel$ even when the neural network weights $\ModelParameters$ remain untouched. The operational testing distribution $\OperationalTestDistribution$ is therefore an inseparable component of the quantity being estimated.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The formal integral over the closed-loop trajectory distribution, including the plant transition kernel and the permission map, is developed in @sec-appendix-ml-trajectory-distribution.
:::

In test engineering, the abstract distribution $\OperationalTestDistribution$ is operationalized through a **stratified test matrix**[^fn-design-experiments-blocking] across controllable parameters, systematically varying payload mass, approach speed, illumination, and initial spatial standoff, while logging uncontrollable environmental parameters such as ambient temperature and floor friction. Unstratified, naive random sampling across the parameter space is fundamentally inadequate because it oversamples benign nominal states while leaving critical boundary regions unvisited. Each stratum of the matrix (one payload, one approach speed, one plate position) is then its own population for the statistical bounds that follow, with its own $\OperationalTestDistribution$ and its own success probability; a claim about the whole matrix needs explicit weights across strata, which the evaluation record of @sec-evaluation-logs declares before the first run.

[^fn-design-experiments-blocking]: **Design of Experiments**\index{Design of experiments!stratified test matrix}: Fisher's agricultural field trials introduced randomization and blocking so that variation in the soil could not masquerade as a treatment effect [@fisher1935design]. A stratified test matrix blocks on payload, approach speed, and lighting for the same reason, and randomizing the run order keeps winding heat and spring relaxation from entering the comparison as if they were properties of the policy (@sec-evaluation-policy-comparison).

::: {#dfn-evaluation-closed-loop-estimand .callout-definition title="Closed-loop evaluation estimand"}

***Closed-loop evaluation estimand***\index{Closed-loop evaluation estimand!definition}\index{Evaluation estimand!definition} is the expected physical task outcome $\TrialSuccessProbability(\OperationalTestDistribution) = \mathbb{E}_{\TrialCondition \sim \OperationalTestDistribution}[\EvaluationPredicate(\text{Traj}(\TrialCondition))]$ defined over the joint distribution of initial states, mechanical plant wear, environmental physics, frozen policy weights, and evaluation predicates:
$$\TrialCondition = (\MechanicalPlantState_0, \EnvironmentParameters, \PlantParameters, \pi_\ModelParameters, \TerminationProtocol) \sim \OperationalTestDistribution$$
rather than an intrinsic property of the neural policy weights evaluated in isolation.

1.  **Significance**: In static machine learning, held-out accuracy is treated as a property of the model $\pi_\ModelParameters$. In physical AI, substituting a worn tire, letting battery voltage sag, or shifting ambient illuminance alters the physical state transition function without changing a single weight. The sampling distribution of operational conditions $\OperationalTestDistribution$ is an inseparable part of the quantity being estimated.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike open-loop validation metrics (such as validation loss, cosine similarity, or mean squared trajectory error) that score predictions against frozen recorded states, the closed-loop estimand integrates over the endogenous feedback loop where past actions physically move the machine, directly changing the future sensor observations it receives.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reporting a single success rate percentage without predeclaring the support, density, and environmental bounds of the test distribution $\OperationalTestDistribution$. Any physical policy can be made arbitrarily successful by testing exclusively in benign, unperturbed states.

:::

### Hardware instance variance and environmental unobservables

The physical mechanisms that alter $\TrialCondition$ between trials operate independently of the policy. A mobile manipulator exhibits this dispersion across two major sources: **hardware instance variance** across individual machines and **environmental unobservables** in the operating workspace.

First, hardware instance variance reflects the physical reality that robotic production lines do not manufacture identical copies. Even within the same manufacturing batch, robots exhibit unit-to-unit mechanical tolerances:

- **Transmission lost motion and compliance**: Strain-wave (harmonic) drives in robot arms feature zero backlash at the gear mesh by design; their dominant mechanical nonlinearities are torsional compliance and hysteresis, while shaft couplings or planetary stages elsewhere in the drivetrain add true backlash [@harmonicdrive2006csf]. These physical properties differ across units and grow with mechanical wear. Under high-frequency direction reversals, they introduce nonlinear hysteresis and phase lag that can destabilize tight neural feedback loops. Consequently, rigorous qualification campaigns characterize each unit's lost motion and joint stiffness directly on an inspection bench rather than assuming nominal catalog values.
- **Structural link compliance**: Elastic link deflection under payload varies across chassis assemblies, shifting the true Tool Center Point (TCP)\index{Tool center point} away from kinematic calculations derived from rigid-body nominals.
- **Sensor assembly misalignments**: Camera brackets and depth sensor mountings deviate from their computer-aided design nominals, introducing systematic coordinate frame offsets between the sensor frame $\CameraReferenceFrame$ and the robot base frame $\BodyReferenceFrame$ that require empirical extrinsic calibration on each individual machine.
- **Actuator electrical variance**: Motor phase resistances and torque constants ($\MotorTorqueConstant$) vary across stator windings within manufacturing tolerance bands. Furthermore, as the battery discharges\index{State of charge (SoC)}, the motor drivers lose voltage headroom against back-electromotive force (back-EMF)\index{Back-EMF}, shifting the torque-speed curve\index{Torque-speed curve} downward and diminishing instantaneous acceleration authority.

Second, environmental unobservables alter physical interaction dynamics without changing camera pixels in ways that a neural network can easily recognize. Ambient daylight shifting across a warehouse alters illuminance, causing camera auto-exposure routines to lengthen shutter times and inducing severe motion blur during base turns. Direct solar glare at dawn or dusk saturates complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensor arrays, washing out optical contrast around the latch interface. On the floor, dust accumulation and ambient humidity alter the tire-floor friction coefficient ($\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$), lengthening braking distances and corrupting wheel odometry. Within the manipulator arm, repeated door openings generate Joule heating ($\WindingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance$)\index{Joule heating} in motor windings and warm harmonic drive lubricants, decreasing viscous damping and causing thermal expansion across structural links. Consequently, the tool center point meets the latch with a millimeter-scale spatial offset on a hot afternoon compared to a cold morning. A policy evaluated across twenty trials on Unit 01 in the morning can fail completely when tested on Unit 02 in the afternoon, despite running identical frozen weights.

Trial reset procedures introduce another major source of unintended drift in $\TrialCondition$. When human operators reposition the mobile base after a difficult or aborted run, subconscious bias often leads them to favor forgiving, nominal configurations, systematically excising difficult boundary states from the sample. Conversely, an automated reset routine that drives the identical recovery path repeatedly heats actuator windings cyclically, introducing progressive thermal degradation across runs. Worst of all, an operator who catches a stumbling robot mid-fall and discards the run as an invalid trial erases the most informative corner-case failures from the evaluation record.

Statistical evaluation must therefore maintain a strict distinction between sampling variation and shifts in the underlying estimand. When $\TrialCount$ independent trials are drawn from a stationary distribution $\OperationalTestDistribution$, the sample proportion $\ObservedSuccessFraction = \frac{1}{\TrialCount} \sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount \TrialCompletionIndicator_i$ fluctuates around the true expectation $\TrialSuccessProbability(\OperationalTestDistribution)$ due to ordinary binomial noise, which standard statistical estimators bound. However, loading a payload onto the tote rack or moving the door's strike plate transitions the experiment to an entirely different distribution $\ShiftedTestDistribution$ with its own success probability $\TrialSuccessProbability(\ShiftedTestDistribution)$. Pooling runs across these two conditions without declaring their sampling weights conflates distinct physical configurations into an uninterpretable average. Independent draws from a predeclared mixture support a claim about that mixture; a quota-based stratified matrix instead requires separate inference within each cell and explicit weighting for an aggregate claim.

### Intervention-based physical metrics

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-jam-reset
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESET SHARE OF A JAMMED DOOR RUN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Reset Latency item in @sec-evaluation-what-measured.
# │ Show: the share of test-cell occupancy a jammed-latch reset consumes.
# │ How: share = t_jam_reset / (t_run + t_jam_reset); t_run matches DoorCycle.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_time, fmt_percent, check

class JamReset:
    """Occupancy share of a manual reset after a jammed latch."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_run = 25.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; door run, same as DoorCycle.t_run
    t_jam_reset = 60.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; clear a jammed pin, recalibrate, return to standoff

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    reset_share = (t_jam_reset / (t_run + t_jam_reset)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.70 < reset_share < 0.72, "Jammed-latch reset should take about 71 percent of occupancy")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_run_str = fmt_time(t_run, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_jam_reset_str = fmt_time(t_jam_reset, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    reset_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(reset_share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Summarizing physical performance with a single binary success rate obscures critical engineering distinctions. Consider four divergent operational outcomes during a door-opening task:

- A policy proposes an excessive contact force, but the permission path clips the command, allowing the door to open smoothly while remaining within mechanical limits.
- The permission path detects an impending joint limit and halts the manipulator entirely, preserving hardware safety while leaving the task incomplete.
- A human safety operator intervenes via remote teleoperation to clear a jammed latch pin, after which the robot resumes autonomous execution and completes the run.
- The raw policy executes the entire trajectory unassisted, completing the manipulation task within nominal limits without intervention.

These scenarios represent fundamentally different system capabilities. Every protective actor in them other than the human operator is the permission path, acting in one of three ways (clipping a proposal, replacing it, or stopping the machine). The first scenario demonstrates a well-functioning integrated machine where the permission path's clips compensate for raw proposer imperfections. The second protects the hardware at the expense of task completion. The third achieves the objective only by drawing on costly human labor. The fourth demonstrates genuine proposer autonomy.

Evaluating physical AI systems therefore requires decomposing performance into three independent channels: whole-machine task completion within operational limits, raw proposer autonomy, and supervisory intervention frequency. The task-completion rate, the fraction of trials whose outcome $\TrialCompletionIndicator_i$ (defined in the first item below) equals 1, measures the first channel. The autonomous completion rate measures the second, and mean time between interventions and intervention density measure the third. Reset latency belongs to no channel; it prices what each outcome costs the test cell. Runtime safety adjustments remain an intended feature of robust system architecture, so a small corrective clip by the permission path should not brand a completed run as a system failure. Nevertheless, tracking proposer autonomy separately reveals how often the learned model attempts to violate physical boundaries. Telemetry pipelines must log adjustments, command rejections, protective stops, and human overrides using predeclared event-counting rules, ensuring that a sustained safety clamp over several seconds is recorded as a single event rather than hundreds of spurious high-frequency faults.

1. **Autonomous completion rate (ACR)**\index{Autonomous completion rate!definition}: Let ${\TrialInterventionCount}_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ be the total count of supervisory interventions during trial $\EvaluationTrialIndex$, whether initiated by human safety operators, the permission path's clips and stops, or emergency tripwires, and let $\TrialCompletionIndicator_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote goal achievement within the execution deadline $\CompletionDeadline$. The unassisted autonomous success indicator is:
   $$\UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = \IndicatorFunction(\TrialCompletionIndicator_i = 1 \land {\TrialInterventionCount}_i = 0)$$
   ACR is the sample proportion of trials completed entirely without supervisory intervention:
   $$\text{ACR} = \frac{1}{\TrialCount} \sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount \UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = \frac{\UnassistedCompletionCount}{\TrialCount}$$
   ACR measures strict raw proposer autonomy: a single recorded intervention forces $\UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = 0$. In contrast, the whole-machine outcome $\TrialCompletionIndicator_i$ can remain $1$ when the permission path clips the proposer's commands and the task still completes within service bounds.

2. **Mean time between interventions (MTBI)**\index{Mean time between interventions!definition}: For any declared intervention class, MTBI quantifies the mean active operating duration between supervisory events:
   $$\SupervisoryMtbi = \frac{\CampaignActiveTime}{\TotalInterventionCount} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount {\TrialRunTime}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount {\TrialInterventionCount}_i}$$
   where ${\TrialRunTime}_i$ is the active operating duration of trial $\EvaluationTrialIndex$ and $\TotalInterventionCount = \sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount {\TrialInterventionCount}_i$ is the total count of recorded interventions within that class. MTBI reflects the operational burden imposed by supervisory systems. Frequent automated filter adjustments signal aggressive policy proposals or model distribution shift, whereas frequent manual recoveries directly drive up staffing costs. Neither a favorable MTBI nor an absence of physical damage proves that a policy is ready for unattended deployment.

3. **Intervention density ($\InterventionDensity$)**\index{Intervention density!definition}: In spatial navigation and continuous trajectory tracking, interventions must be normalized against physical travel distance or discrete execution steps:
   $$\InterventionDensity = \frac{\TotalInterventionCount}{\sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount \TrialPathDistance_i} \quad [\text{interventions per kilometer}] \quad \text{or} \quad \InterventionDensity = 1{,}000 \times \frac{\TotalInterventionCount}{\sum_{i=1}^\TrialCount \TrialControlStepCount} \quad [\text{interventions per } 1{,}000 \text{ steps}]$$
   where $\TrialPathDistance_i$ is the physical path distance traversed during trial $\EvaluationTrialIndex$, and $\TrialControlStepCount$ is the number of control cycles executed. Normalizing by exposure makes intervention rates comparable across routes or operating conditions. Locating concentrated degradation also requires retaining each event’s location and condition and comparing these rates across strata, such as narrow doorways or tight mechanical latches.

4. **Reset latency ($\TrialResetLatency$)**\index{Reset latency!definition}: In physical qualification campaigns, the primary bottleneck in testing throughput is governed by the time required to restore the robot and workspace after a trial completes or aborts:
   $$\TrialResetLatency = \PhysicalRestoreTime + \ResetCalibrationTime + \TelemetryFlushTime$$
   The standard door-opening run requires `{python} JamReset.t_run_str` of active execution. While its nominal reset cycle is brief (@sec-evaluation-trial-costs), a run that jams the latch pin requires an operator intervention of approximately `{python} JamReset.t_jam_reset_str` (illustrative) to clear the jammed pin, recalibrate joint encoders, and return the mobile base to its initial standoff pose. For jammed runs, this manual reset consumes `{python} JamReset.reset_share_pct_str` of total test-cell occupancy. High reset latencies create organizational pressure to cut corners, for instance by skipping required motor thermal cooldowns or manually nudging the robot into easier initial poses, and each shortcut breaks the statistical stationarity of the campaign.

Engineers must not conflate MTBI with mean time between failures (MTBF). While an MTBF metric tracks functional breakdowns or mechanical failures, MTBI, ACR, and $\InterventionDensity$ capture supervisory burden and proposer autonomy within an operating envelope. A robot fleet can maintain an unblemished record of zero hardware damage simply because vigilant human safety drivers or a conservative permission path intervene whenever an unsafe state nears. Recording a run that was truncated or guided by external supervision as an unassisted operational success masks policy shortcomings behind the protective capability of the safety system. @Sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes shows why such runs are censored observations and names this error the censored trial fallacy.

Rigorous evaluation protocols decouple these metrics so that engineers can observe the trade-offs between safety filtering, autonomous capability, and operational throughput. Defining these outcome channels establishes what quantities must be recorded across experimental trials; the subsequent challenge is designing the closed-loop evaluation harness to expose these behaviors systematically under dynamic feedback.

## Closed-Loop Dynamics {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics}

In standard deep learning workflows, model evaluation centers on empirical risk minimization over a static, held-out validation dataset $\ValidationDataset = \{(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i)\}_{i=1}^\EvaluationSampleCount$:
$$\ValidationLoss(\ModelParameters) = \frac{1}{\EvaluationSampleCount} \sum_{i=1}^\EvaluationSampleCount \LossFunction(\ParameterizedPredictor(\ModelInput_i), \ExampleLabel_i)$$
Whether the target metric is Top-1 classification accuracy, next-token perplexity, an F1 score, or coordinate regression loss, the evaluation pipeline remains fundamentally passive and decoupled. The underlying data-generating process operates strictly feedforward and memoryless with respect to the model's outputs: mispredicting sample $\ExampleIndex$ exerts zero causal influence on sample $\ExampleIndex+1$ ($\partial \ModelInput_{i+1} / \partial \ModelPrediction_i = 0$).

Transporting this static paradigm to physical control creates the **offline evaluation illusion**, the unfounded assumption that lower validation loss, higher action cosine similarity, or smaller Mean Squared Error (MSE) on logged data guarantees superior physical execution. Offline loss metrics of the form $\ValidationLoss(\ModelParameters) = \frac{1}{\EvaluationSampleCount} \sum_{i=1}^\EvaluationSampleCount \|\DemonstratorAction_i - \pi_\ModelParameters(\MechanicalPlantState_i^*)\|^2$ evaluate candidate predictions exclusively along frozen demonstrator trajectories. Empirical studies demonstrate this failure directly. In controlled benchmarks across simulated and physical manipulation tasks, the training checkpoint exhibiting the lowest validation loss performed substantially worse during closed-loop rollouts than alternative checkpoints, with task success frequently rising even as validation loss climbed [@mandlekar2021matters].

The decoupling that justifies offline scoring vanishes in physical AI. Admitted policy actions cross the causal boundary into mass, momentum, and non-smooth contact mechanics. Instead of assigning categorical labels, the policy outputs forces, torques, and velocity setpoints that physically perturb the plant, endogenously generating future sensory observations through the system dynamics ($\MechanicalPlantState_{t+1} = \DiscretePlantDynamics(\MechanicalPlantState_t, \AdmittedControlCommand_t)$). These commands interact continuously with inertia, friction, and mechanical backlash. Consequently, a navigation policy can track recorded demonstrator trajectories with negligible regression error during offline playback, yet exhaust the vehicle's entire lateral clearance against a warehouse rack before traversing a third of the aisle. The failure stems directly from what each evaluation regime feeds back to the policy.

In an **open-loop evaluation**\index{Open-loop evaluation!definition}, a candidate policy $\pi_\ModelParameters$ is scored across a static dataset of recorded demonstrations $\DemonstrationDataset = \{(\MechanicalPlantState_t^*, \DemonstratorAction_t)\}_{t=1}^{\BehaviorCloningHorizon}$. At each discrete timestep $\ControlStepIndex$, the policy receives an expert state $\MechanicalPlantState_t^*$ and predicts an action $\PredictedPolicyAction_t = \pi_\ModelParameters(\MechanicalPlantState_t^*)$. A standard loss function, such as mean squared error or cross-entropy, measures the discrepancy between $\PredictedPolicyAction_t$ and the recorded expert action $\DemonstratorAction_t$. At timestep $\ControlStepIndex+1$, the harness feeds the next recorded state $\MechanicalPlantState_{t+1}^*$ directly from storage. The policy's predicted action $\PredictedPolicyAction_t$ is discarded without ever executing on physical hardware, ensuring that the incoming state sequence remains strictly independent of prior predictions ($\partial \MechanicalPlantState_{t+1}^* / \partial \PredictedPolicyAction_t = \ZeroVector$). In a **closed-loop evaluation**\index{Closed-loop evaluation!definition}, the policy proposes an action $\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} = \pi_\ModelParameters(\MechanicalPlantState_t)$ based on runtime sensory feedback. The system's deterministic permission path validates this proposal against the current plant state and safety invariants, dispatching an approved command $\AdmittedControlCommand_t$ (or an intervention fallback) to the actuators. The plant then advances according to physical dynamics, yielding $\MechanicalPlantState_{t+1} = \DiscretePlantDynamics(\MechanicalPlantState_t, \AdmittedControlCommand_t)$. Every admitted command alters the physical state and determines all subsequent sensory inputs, crossing the causal boundary.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_as.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Act-to-Sense feedback edge."}
*Admitted actions choose the next observation.*
:::

### Compounding error and kinematic integration {#sec-evaluation-compounding-error}

A neural policy exhibiting negligible open-loop validation loss can destabilize and drive a physical robot off course within seconds. Open-loop evaluation evaluates actions strictly along demonstrator trajectories, resetting the robot's input state to nominal expert measurements at every clock cycle. During closed-loop rollouts, however, the policy's admitted actions drive the physical plant, meaning that small tracking discrepancies immediately distort subsequent sensory observations.

This discrepancy takes a formal worst-case structure, as derived in @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability. If a policy deviates from expert actions with probability at most $\SingleStepImitationError$ per step on recorded expert states, open-loop evaluation across a horizon of $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$ steps accumulates an expected cost bounded by $\BehaviorCloningHorizon\SingleStepImitationError$. In closed loop, however, an early deviation can steer the robot into unvisited regions of the state space for the remainder of the trajectory, driving the cumulative imitation cost to scale as $\BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError$ (@eq-data-quadratic-drift). For systems engineers, the operational implication is stark: an open-loop benchmark can understate closed-loop task divergence by a factor proportional to the operating horizon. While this theoretical bound governs zero-one decision divergence rather than unbounded metrics like contact force or structural yield, classical kinematics reveals the underlying physical mechanism: uncorrected heading and steering biases integrate forward into macroscopic lateral displacements that rapidly exhaust the robot's clearance envelope.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HEADING BIAS AGAINST THE AISLE'S SIDE CLEARANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop,
# │          and the takeaways.
# │ Show: where a persistent 1 degree heading bias of the navigation stack
# │       (not the evaluated latch policy) spends the aisle's side clearance.
# │ How: y(t) = v sin(eps) t; t_impact = W_clear / (v sin(eps)); the side
# │      clearance is (aisle width - machine width) / 2.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_time, fmt_angle, fmt_math, sci_latex, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class AisleDrift:
    """Closed-loop drift of a biased navigation policy on the running machine's aisle."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit
    clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative; side clearance each side
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    aisle_length = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative; site geometry
    machine_width = RM.footprint_width  # category: illustrative; base footprint
    heading_offset_deg = 1.0  # category: illustrative; persistent heading bias

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps = math.radians(heading_offset_deg)
    eps_q = eps * radian
    angular_mse = (eps_q**2).to(radian**2)  # open-loop score on recorded centerline states
    t_impact = (clearance / (v * math.sin(eps))).to(ureg.second)
    x_impact = (v * t_impact).to(ureg.meter)
    aisle_fraction = (x_impact / aisle_length).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Drive limit is not 1.5 m/s")
    check(abs(clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Side clearance is not 0.15 m")
    check(abs(((aisle_width - machine_width) / 2 - clearance).to(ureg.meter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Side clearance must equal (aisle - machine) / 2")
    check(abs(aisle_length.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, "Aisle length is not 30 m")
    check(abs(x_impact.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 8.6) < 0.05, "Clearance should be spent in about 8.6 m")
    check(abs(t_impact.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 5.73) < 0.005, "Clearance should be spent in about 5.7 s")
    check(aisle_fraction < 1 / 3, "Prose says less than a third of the aisle")
    check(abs(heading_offset_deg - 1.0) < 1e-12, "Prose, fig-cap, and fig-alt state a 1.0 degree heading offset")
    check(abs(angular_mse.magnitude - 3.05e-4) < 5e-7, "fig-alt states an angular MSE of 3.05e-4 rad^2")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, precision=2)
    aisle_width_str = fmt_length(aisle_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    aisle_length_str = fmt_length(aisle_length, precision=0)
    machine_width_str = fmt_length(machine_width, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    clearance_cm_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=ureg.centimeter, precision=0)
    t_impact_str = fmt_time(t_impact, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    x_impact_str = fmt_length(x_impact, precision=1)
    eps_rad_str = fmt_angle(eps_q, precision=5)
    angular_mse_math = fmt_math(rf"{sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2")
    angular_mse_eq = fmt_math(
        rf"\text{{MSE}}_{{\HeadingAngle}} = ({fmt(eps, precision=5)})^2 \approx {sci_latex(angular_mse.magnitude)}\text{{ rad}}^2"
    )
```

A policy whose own actions displace it from its training distribution is the second law at work on a test bench, and evaluation must quantify what that displacement costs on physical hardware. Because the mobile manipulator's base remains stationary during door manipulation trials, the platform's warehouse navigation stack supplies the clearest illustration of kinematic accumulation. Consider the base traversing a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle at its `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit, where the nominal expert trajectory tracks the centerline with heading $\HeadingAngle^* = 0\text{ rad}$ and lateral offset $\BaseLateralPosition^* = 0\text{ m}$. Suppose the candidate navigation policy possesses a systematic heading bias of $\FiniteChange\HeadingAngle = 1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) at every control step. The deterministic permission path admits each individual velocity command because, in isolation, a one-degree heading adjustment remains dynamically feasible while lateral clearance persists.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ How a policy's own actions shift the states it visits away from the demonstrator's occupancy is established in @sec-data-covariate-shift.
:::

In an open-loop evaluation, the policy receives the demonstrator state $\MechanicalPlantState_t^* = ({\BaseLongitudinalPosition}_t^*, 0, 0)$ at each step and predicts forward velocity with a $1.0^\circ$ steering offset. The offline scoring pipeline records a mean absolute angular error of $1.0^\circ$ (`{python} AisleDrift.eps_rad_str`) and a mean squared error of `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_eq`.[^fn-math-openloop-mse] The small number reflects radians squared, not the lesson. What matters is that the replay score stays at that same per-step value however long the aisle is, because each next input returns to the centerline and the error never accumulates. During closed-loop execution, however, the robot's physical movement reflects previously admitted commands, allowing uncorrected heading errors to integrate continuously. Under planar unicycle kinematics[^fn-unicycle-model-drift] ($\BaseLateralVelocity = \BaseForwardSpeed \sin \HeadingAngle \approx \BaseForwardSpeed \FiniteChange\HeadingAngle$), a persistent angular offset integrates directly into a lateral displacement that grows linearly with the time $\DriftElapsedTime$ since the base left the centerline:
$$\BaseLateralPosition(\DriftElapsedTime) = \int_0^{\DriftElapsedTime} \BaseForwardSpeed \sin \FiniteChange\HeadingAngle \, d\IntegrationDummyTime \approx \BaseForwardSpeed \FiniteChange\HeadingAngle \DriftElapsedTime$$
If the policy exhibits a persistent yaw-rate bias $\BaseYawRateBias$ (steering drift) rather than a fixed angular offset, the heading angle itself grows linearly over time ($\HeadingAngle(\DriftElapsedTime) = \int_0^{\DriftElapsedTime} \BaseYawRateBias \, d\IntegrationDummyTime = \BaseYawRateBias \DriftElapsedTime$). Integrating forward velocity $\BaseForwardSpeed$ then yields a cumulative lateral deviation that compounds quadratically in time:
$$\BaseLateralPosition(\DriftElapsedTime) = \int_0^{\DriftElapsedTime} \BaseForwardSpeed \sin(\BaseYawRateBias \IntegrationDummyTime) \, d\IntegrationDummyTime \approx \frac{1}{2} \BaseForwardSpeed \BaseYawRateBias \DriftElapsedTime^2$$
This quadratic growth resembles the $\BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError$ imitation bound, but the two characterize distinct phenomena. The kinematic derivation integrates a systematic yaw-rate bias through continuous dynamics, whereas the imitation bound accounts for accumulated discrete decision costs under distribution shift. Both show small, bounded errors accumulating polynomially over an operational horizon. Neither excludes the worse case that @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability described, in which a smooth imitator of a stable expert can compound its errors exponentially with horizon; the aisle example simply does not need that mechanism to fail.

For the constant $1.0^\circ$ heading bias, the mobile base spans `{python} AisleDrift.machine_width_str` within a `{python} AisleDrift.aisle_width_str` aisle. This geometry leaves $\LateralClearance =$ `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_cm_str` of lateral clearance to the storage racks on either side. At full drive velocity, the kinematic drift consumes this safety buffer at:
$$\ClearanceExhaustionTime = \frac{\LateralClearance}{\BaseForwardSpeed \sin \FiniteChange\HeadingAngle},$$ {#eq-eval-clearance-time}
which evaluates to `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str`, after just `{python} AisleDrift.x_impact_str` of forward travel, less than a third of the way through the aisle. The same heading offset that replay scores at an angular mean squared error of `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_math`, because each next input returns to the recorded centerline, spends the entire `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_str` side clearance in the physical loop (@fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop). The computed point is the unmitigated collision horizon. To halt before impact, the runtime permission path must intervene earlier, allowing for qualified detection, command and actuation response, and stopping motion. A protective stop makes strict proposer autonomy fail while preserving protection; an unprotected rack strike fails protection as well. Both expose a limitation of the policy that offline evaluation rated as near-flawless.

[^fn-math-openloop-mse]: **Mean Masking of Steering Spikes**\index{Evaluation!metric masking}: Averaging squared steering error over thousands of straight-aisle frames also hides a brief, large prediction spike, which barely moves the mean. Whether such a spike matters depends on whether its integrated motion spends the clearance before the permission path responds, a question only a plant and timing model can answer.

[^fn-unicycle-model-drift]: **Unicycle Model**\index{Unicycle model!lateral drift}: The simplest planar vehicle model, in which pose $(\BaseLongitudinalPosition, \BaseLateralPosition, \HeadingAngle)$ evolves as $\BaseLongitudinalVelocity = \BaseForwardSpeed\cos\HeadingAngle$, $\BaseLateralVelocity = \BaseForwardSpeed\sin\HeadingAngle$, $\BaseHeadingRate = \YawRate$. This formulation captures the essential nonholonomic constraint of the aisle: because a wheeled base cannot translate instantaneously sideways, any heading discrepancy directly translates forward velocity toward the rack.

This warehouse scenario highlights the two structural mechanisms that cause open-loop validation metrics\index{Open-loop evaluation!closed-loop gap} to decouple from physical performance:

1. **State integration across time**: Static evaluation cannot integrate persistent control errors into physical displacements. By resetting the robot's input state to an expert demonstration at every clock cycle, offline scoring obscures error accumulation. In closed-loop deployment, however, the state at timestep $\ControlStepIndex$ represents the unrolled composition of all prior control actions:
   $$\MechanicalPlantState_t = \DiscretePlantDynamics(\DiscretePlantDynamics(\dots \DiscretePlantDynamics(\MechanicalPlantState_0, \AdmittedControlCommand_0)\dots, \AdmittedControlCommand_{t-2}), \AdmittedControlCommand_{t-1})$$
   A persistent heading bias does not require an algorithmic flaw; physical phenomena like asymmetric tire wear, mast vibration, uneven payload distribution, or floor camber routinely introduce systematic offsets.
2. **Covariate shift into unmodeled states**: Static benchmarks cannot evaluate how a policy behaves once early errors steer the plant away from nominal trajectories. The very first uncorrected action shifts the base from the expert state $\MechanicalPlantState_1^*$ to an unvisited state $\MechanicalPlantState_1$. Once the base drifts even a few centimeters off the centerline, it enters operating states completely absent from $\DemonstrationDataset$. Because offline metrics are evaluated exclusively along demonstrator states where $\BaseLateralPosition = 0\text{ m}$, they provide zero empirical evidence regarding policy behavior when $\BaseLateralPosition \neq 0\text{ m}$. Lacking training on corrective maneuvers, the policy often generates larger prediction errors in these off-nominal regimes, precipitating rapid divergence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Compounding covariate shift, and the recovery experience a fixed demonstration archive lacks, are established in @sec-training-recovery-experience.
:::

::: {#fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open vs. closed loop divergence**: A persistent $1.0^\circ$ heading offset gives `{python} AisleDrift.angular_mse_math` angular mean squared error on recorded centerline states. On the mobile manipulator's aisle, the navigation stack's admitted motion with that fixed heading drifts linearly and reaches the `{python} AisleDrift.clearance_str` side clearance after `{python} AisleDrift.t_impact_str` at the `{python} AisleDrift.v_str` drive limit. The example concerns the navigation stack, not the latch policy under evaluation." fig-alt="Two-panel aisle example. Left: recorded-state replay scores a constant one-degree heading offset with angular mean squared error 3.05 times 10 to the minus four radians squared and resets the next input to the recorded centerline. Right: if that heading persists in a physical rollout at 1.5 meters per second, lateral drift grows linearly and reaches the 15-centimeter side clearance after about 5.7 seconds, 8.6 meters along the aisle. Policy proposals pass through the permission path before the plant moves."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPEN-LOOP REPLAY VS. CLOSED-LOOP DRIFT (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop
# │ Goal:    show why a heading error that is invisible offline spends clearance
# │ Show:    lateral offset against forward position, replay beside physical loop
# │ How:     one heading offset drives both panels and both numbers;
# │          speed and clearance come from the aisle via calc-evaluation-aisle-heading-drift
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

COLORS = viz.COLORS

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario parameters) ────────────────────────────────────────────
HEADING_OFFSET_DEG = AisleDrift.heading_offset_deg  # category: illustrative; from the LEGO cell
CLEARANCE_M = AisleDrift.clearance.to(ureg.meter).magnitude  # category: illustrative; AISLE.side_clearance
SPEED_MS = AisleDrift.v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude  # category: illustrative; RM.base.max_velocity (drive limit)
REACH_M = 10.0  # category: chosen; plot extent, the first third of the aisle

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
theta = math.radians(HEADING_OFFSET_DEG)
angular_mse = theta**2  # rad^2, the offline error signal
exhausted_m = CLEARANCE_M / math.tan(theta)  # where the drift reaches clearance
exhausted_s = exhausted_m / SPEED_MS

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, (ax_a, ax_b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8), sharey=True)
x = np.linspace(0, REACH_M, 400)

ax_a.plot(x, np.zeros_like(x), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.4)
ax_a.plot(np.arange(0, REACH_M, 2), np.zeros(int(REACH_M // 2)), "o", ms=5, color=COLORS["BlueLine"])
ax_a.text(
    0.6,
    0.107,
    "Each next input returns to\nthe recorded centerline",
    fontsize=9,
    va="center",
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc="white", ec=COLORS["grid"], lw=1.0),
)
ax_a.text(0.6, 0.030, f"Angular MSE: {angular_mse:.2e} rad$^2$".replace("e-04", r" $\times$ 10$^{-4}$"), fontsize=9, color=COLORS["BlueLine"])

ax_b.plot(x, x * math.tan(theta), color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=2.4)
ax_b.axhline(0.0, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
ax_b.axvline(exhausted_m, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.0, linestyle=(0, (1, 2)))
ax_b.plot([exhausted_m], [CLEARANCE_M], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["RedLine"], zorder=5)
ax_b.text(
    exhausted_m - 0.35, CLEARANCE_M - 0.075, f"Clearance exhausted\nat {exhausted_s:.1f} s", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["RedLine"], ha="right", va="top"
)
ax_b.text(0.6, 0.182, rf"$y_{{\mathrm{{base}}}} = x_{{\mathrm{{base}}}}\,\tan$({HEADING_OFFSET_DEG:.0f}°) under fixed heading", fontsize=9)

for ax, title, lx, lha in ((ax_a, "(a) Recorded-state replay", REACH_M - 0.15, "right"), (ax_b, "(b) Physical closed loop", 0.6, "left")):
    ax.axhline(CLEARANCE_M, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.2, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
    ax.text(lx, CLEARANCE_M + 0.006, f"{CLEARANCE_M * 100:.0f} cm clearance", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["RedLine"], ha=lha, va="bottom")
    ax.set_xlim(0, REACH_M)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.03, 0.225)
    ax.set_xticks(range(0, int(REACH_M) + 1, 2))
    ax.set_xlabel("Forward position (m)")
    ax.text(0.0, 1.02, title, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

ax_a.set_yticks([0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20])
ax_a.set_ylabel("Lateral offset (m)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

### Contact discontinuities and metric masking {#sec-evaluation-non-lipschitz-contact}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-stiff-contact
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STIFF-CONTACT RESIDUAL VERSUS FREE-SPACE RESIDUAL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Why action mean squared error fails" in
# │          @sec-evaluation-non-lipschitz-contact.
# │ Show: the reaction force a small commanded penetration attempts against a
# │       hypothetical stiff surface (not the running machine's latch).
# │ How: dF = k_contact * dx (linear spring).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_force, fmt_math, sci_latex, check

class StiffContact:
    """Force a millimeter-scale residual attempts against a stiff surface."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    k_contact = 5e5 * ureg.newton / ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; hypothetical stiff surface
    dx = 2.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative; tracking residual / commanded penetration

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dF = (k_contact * dx).to(newton)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dF.to(newton).magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-6, "2 mm into 5e5 N/m should attempt 1,000 N")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    k_contact_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(k_contact.to(ureg.newton / ureg.meter).magnitude, precision=0) + r"\text{ N/m}")
    dx_str = fmt_length(dx, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    dF_str = fmt_force(dF, precision=0, commas=True)
```

Physical contact introduces severe mathematical and dynamical discontinuities. As an end-effector engages a door latch, unconstrained free-space kinematics instantaneously transition into constrained contact mechanics characterized by impact, stick, or slip. In classical rigid-body mechanics, collision produces discontinuous velocity jumps ($\PostImpactNormalVelocity \ne \PreImpactNormalVelocity$), while Coulomb friction creates set-valued reaction forces ($\CoulombFrictionForce \in [-\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce, \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce]$). Because these transitions violate Lipschitz continuity (a bound on how much the dynamics can change per unit change in state), infinitesimally small variations in spatial state produce disproportionately large, discontinuous changes in physical dynamics. Although mechanical compliance and structural damping distribute impact forces across small time windows in real hardware, aggregate offline loss metrics obscure the critical physical consequences of crossing contact boundaries:

1. **Action cosine similarity ignores operational magnitude**: In representation learning and behavior modeling, action cosine similarity:
   $$\text{Cosine}(\PredictedPolicyAction, \DemonstratorAction) = \frac{\PredictedPolicyAction^\top \DemonstratorAction}{\|\PredictedPolicyAction\| \|\DemonstratorAction\|}$$
   evaluates directional alignment between predicted and expert commands. At a physical contact interface, however, directional alignment alone is catastrophic because cosine metrics discard vector magnitude entirely. A policy proposal achieving 0.999 cosine similarity that commands 25 percent insufficient force fails to overcome the latch's mechanical preload and static friction, stalling against the mechanism and halting the task. Conversely, a command with identical 0.999 similarity that commands 150 percent of the required force severely overloads the contact interface, risking an immediate trigger of the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` protective tripwire. Whether hardware damage occurs depends on structural compliance, pre-contact kinetic energy, and joint impedance response; a trip invokes the protective response, whose ability to prevent damage requires qualification under those conditions. A stopped, incomplete run fails the task despite the favorable cosine score.

2. **Action mean squared error equates disparate physical regimes**: In offline supervised regression, Mean Squared Error:
   $$\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{\ActionDimension} \sum_{j=1}^{\ActionDimension} (\PredictedActionComponent_j - \DemonstratorActionComponent_j^*)^2$$
   penalizes every millimeter of tracking residual identically, regardless of physical context. During free-space transit, an end-effector tracking discrepancy of `{python} StiffContact.dx_str` represents a benign perturbation that downstream control easily accommodates. Consider, by contrast, a stiff environmental interface modeled with contact stiffness $\ContactStiffness \approx$ `{python} StiffContact.k_contact_math`. When an unmitigated position controller commands an apparent surface penetration $\PenetrationDepth$, the resulting normal reaction force scales as:
   $$\FiniteChange \NormalContactForce = \ContactStiffness \PenetrationDepth$$
   For an uncorrected `{python} StiffContact.dx_str` penetration residual, this linear relationship demands a reaction force of `{python} StiffContact.dF_str`. While realized loads depend on structural compliance, link elasticity, and active torque limits rather than bare stiffness alone, this calculation highlights the dimensional mismatch: offline MSE treats a benign `{python} StiffContact.dx_str` tracking error in free space identically to a contact error capable of tripping joint protection or damaging gearboxes.

3. **Hardware instance variance amplifies contact bifurcations**: Non-smooth contact mechanics compound the unit-to-unit manufacturing variance analyzed in @sec-evaluation-what-measured. Subtle physical discrepancies across production robots, such as transmission backlash, harmonic drive compliance, and millimeter-level camera-mounting tolerances, shift the physical boundary of the contact interface in Cartesian space. A policy trained on demonstrations recorded on Unit 01 will encounter the latch surface slightly earlier or later when deployed on Unit 02. Because contact transitions are discontinuous, this millimeter-scale spatial displacement triggers immediate operational bifurcations: the manipulator either halts prematurely in free space or collides aggressively with the mechanism frame, causing mechanical jamming that static evaluation over historical logs cannot detect.

The door manipulation benchmark illustrates this failure mechanism directly. An end-effector positioning error of a fraction of a millimeter per step registers as negligible Cartesian deviation on static logs. Against the rigid latch mechanism, however, that small offset acts as a mechanical wedge. The same stiffness relation, $\FiniteChange \NormalContactForce = \ContactStiffness \PenetrationDepth$, now acting sideways, transforms this lateral displacement into a steep reaction force that quickly crosses the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire, triggering an immediate safety abort before the door unlatches.

Conversely, offline benchmarks can also fail through false pessimism when tasks support multimodal solution paths. If a human demonstrator avoided an obstacle by steering left, an open-loop regression metric penalizes an autonomous policy that navigates safely to the right (the multimodal distribution dilemma), even though both trajectories satisfy the closed-loop objective. Static action loss measures divergence from a single historical recording, not functional task completion.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Mode averaging over multimodal demonstrations is established in @sec-training-multimodality-breakdown.
:::

These asymmetries frequently produce rank inversions across candidate models. A policy whose small residual errors concentrate precisely at critical contact boundaries will score lower validation loss than a competitor with larger, yet harmless, errors distributed across free space. When deployed, however, their operational reliability reverses:
$$\ValidationLoss(\pi_{\Glyph{A}}) < \ValidationLoss(\pi_{\Glyph{B}}) \quad \text{yet} \quad \text{ACR}(\pi_{\Glyph{A}}) \ll \text{ACR}(\pi_{\Glyph{B}})$$
Rigorous evaluation campaigns must therefore evaluate autonomous completion rates, force profiles, and contact stability on physical hardware rather than ranking models by average offline loss.

This systemic disconnect separates every standard offline machine learning metric from the physical failure modes it conceals. @Tbl-07-offline-closed-loop-disconnect maps each offline metric to its implicit open-loop assumption, its physical failure mechanism, and the corresponding closed-loop metric required to expose it. Most of the closed-loop measures in its last column are physical quantities the record already logs. The one new measure is time to intervention ($\PolicyTti$\index{Time-to-Intervention!metric}), the elapsed duration from the granting of policy authority to the first permission-path override or safety operator takeover, which measures how long a drifting policy runs before something must stop it. Alongside ACR, MTBI, and $\InterventionDensity$, these execution measures characterize real-world autonomy in ways that static loss calculations cannot.

| Offline metric                     | Open-loop assumption                                             | Why it breaks in closed loop                                                                                                    | Failure on the machine                                                 | Closed-loop measure                                                                                            |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Action mean squared error**      | Small residuals give small path deviations                       | A persistent bias integrates into drift and carries the machine off the demonstrated states                                     | The base spends its rack clearance (stop or strike)                    | Peak deviation from the reference path; time to intervention\index{Time-to-Intervention!metric} ($\PolicyTti$) |
| **Discrete action accuracy**       | Correct labels on logged states give identical execution         | Benign alternatives and boundary excursions cost the same; errors correlated in time are invisible                              | Command chatter and joint over-torque                                  | Peak jerk; adherence to actuator torque limits                                                                 |
| **Cosine similarity**              | Collinear proposals give stable paths                            | Magnitude is ignored, so under-actuation stalls against static friction and over-actuation slips                                | The base stalls or slips its wheels; the arm stalls short of the latch | Slip ratio (@sec-appendix-control-slip) and damping (@sec-appendix-control-pid)                                |
| **Negative log-likelihood**        | Likelihood at the expert action captures the action distribution | A unimodal likelihood head averages valid alternatives, such as passing an obstacle on either side, into an invalid mean action | Valid policies rejected; demonstrator noise imitated as jitter         | Closed-loop task success over randomized starts                                                                |
| **Reconstruction or Chamfer loss** | Accurate scene prediction gives safe plans                       | Background pixels outweigh thin obstacles and contact geometry                                                                  | Phantom braking; clipping a cable or a glass partition                 | Measured clearance and its minimum margin                                                                      |

: **Offline metrics and the closed-loop failures they hide**: Each open-loop metric assumes the demonstrator's state distribution is unaffected by policy error; on the machine, biases integrate into drift, valid alternatives are penalized, and shifted states produce boundary violations. {#tbl-07-offline-closed-loop-disconnect tbl-colwidths="[18,20,24,18,20]"}

::: {#psp-evaluation-open-loop-blindness .callout-perspective title="The offline evaluation illusion"}
Offline validation loss, Mean Squared Error (MSE), and action cosine similarity score predictions exclusively along frozen demonstrator trajectories where errors are artificially erased at every clock cycle. Physical closed-loop evaluation exposes accumulated trajectory drift, state distribution shift, and dynamic contact transitions absent from recorded logs. While the worst-case imitation bound ($\CovariateDriftBound$) models decision divergence under distribution shift, kinematic integration and contact mechanics ($\NormalContactForce = \ContactStiffness \PenetrationDepth$) govern physical clearance and reaction forces. A score computed against recorded states cannot see a feedback loop that recording removed.
:::

### The proposal boundary in two-processor architectures {#sec-evaluation-proposal-boundary}

Drift and contact are failures of the plant. A third class of failure lives in the machine's own hardware, and replay misses it for a different reason, because the replay harness runs on the wrong processor. The divide between tensor arithmetic and physical execution is codified in hardware across the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. In the running machine's two-processor architecture, where the learned proposers run on an application processor and the permission path runs on a separate safety microcontroller, replaying sensory traces on the host application processor verifies only whether neural inference completes within allocated memory bandwidth and latency budgets. During real-world execution, however, every candidate action proposal must cross the inter-processor bus to the real-time microcontroller running the deterministic permission path.

When local, high-rate sensor readings reveal that a proposed action violates kinematic, torque, or obstacle-clearance boundaries, the permission path clips or rejects the command. If the active trajectory violates lease deadlines or safety limits, the controller immediately engages a deterministic fallback maneuver. Evaluating an unverified neural policy strictly offline, without the physical plant, real-time bus transport, and safety monitors active in the loop, benchmarks isolated tensor computation rather than operational survivability. What replay on the host cannot see is everything the bus and the microcontroller add: transport delay, a late proposal arriving after its chunk lease has lapsed, a clip that changes the motion the policy expected, and a fallback that takes over mid-task. Shadow operation exposes the first two on real buses without letting the candidate move the machine, and constrained physical testing exposes all four.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The two-processor split, stated as a hypothesis that placement must later test on silicon, is established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How the permission path admits a proposal, corrects it, or transfers authority to a resident fallback is developed in @sec-enforcement-authority-refuse.
:::

Because open-loop metrics cannot certify closed-loop reliability, empirical validation must evaluate the proposer across controlled physical environments. Every deployment setting alters specific elements of the sensorimotor loop by modifying plant dynamics, sensor streaming fidelity, or actuator authority. To structure these trade-offs, @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes categorizes these operational environments by the causal fidelity and failure modes each regime is capable of exposing.

## Evidence Regimes {#sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes}

Before undertaking twenty physical door runs, an engineering team evaluating a robotic latch policy could score candidate predictions against logged human demonstrations, execute them inside a simulated physics environment, run them in shadow mode while a validated controller retains physical authority over the arm, or deploy them directly on the real mechanism with contact tripwires armed. These four configurations constitute the primary **evidence regimes**\index{Evidence regimes!definition} of embodied evaluation, mapped in @fig-07-evidence-regimes and @tbl-07-evidence-regimes across two structural axes: physical realism on the vertical axis (from logged and synthetic feeds up to live hardware) and causal feedback on the horizontal axis (from open loop to closed loop). Each regime establishes a distinct coupling between the policy, its sensory observations, and the underlying physical machine states, meaning each regime supports only a strictly bounded empirical claim. None of these four settings alone reveals how an unassisted policy behaves during open-ended physical deployment, because each environment either breaks the control loop's causal feedback or alters the distribution of states the robot encounters.

### The four evaluation evidence regimes {#sec-evaluation-four-regimes}

The first axis, causal feedback, governs whether a candidate's emitted actions alter future states and subsequent sensor observations ($\partial \MechanicalPlantState_{t+1}/\partial \CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \ne \ZeroVector$), or whether the policy merely reads a prerecorded, invariant sensory stream. In an open-loop configuration, execution errors cannot compound because mistakes never propagate into future inputs. In a closed loop, small policy errors perturb subsequent machine states, accumulating into compounding drift at a rate dictated by system dynamics and closed-loop feedback gains.

The second axis, physical realism, governs whether sensory observations originate from physical transducers interacting with unmodeled contact dynamics, gear backlash, tire slip, and variable illumination ($\PhysicalPlantDynamics$), or instead emerge from a synthetic numerical simulator or static buffer ($\SimulatedPlantDynamics$).

No single testing configuration can maximize both axes simultaneously without exposing expensive hardware, or nearby operators, to an unproven and potentially destructive policy.
