Consequently, each quadrant of @fig-07-evidence-regimes provides rigorous empirical evidence for specific claims while accepting a distinct, structural blind spot.

::: {#fig-07-evidence-regimes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Evaluation evidence regimes**: The regimes vary along causal feedback (open vs. closed loop) and physical realism (logged or synthetic vs. live hardware). Replay cannot observe compounding drift, simulation leaves the reality gap open, shadow operation locks the trajectory to the baseline controller, and constrained testing truncates failures at the constraint boundary $\partial\ConstrainedTestEnvelope$. No single regime tests deployment beyond that boundary." fig-alt="Two-axis schematic with physical realism on the vertical axis, from logged or synthetic up to live hardware, and causal feedback on the horizontal axis, from open loop to closed loop. Four panels. Shadow mode, top left, feeds the real plant's observations to a baseline controller that drives the motors and to a candidate policy whose actions are only logged. Constrained testing, top right, closes the loop from the candidate policy through the permission path to the real plant, inside a red dashed constraint boundary beyond which lies open deployment. Recorded replay, bottom left, feeds a demonstration dataset to the policy and scores the action error, with no path from action back to state. Simulation, bottom right, closes the loop through a simulated plant whose dynamics differ from the real one."}
![](images/svg/fig07_evidence_regimes.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In recorded replay, the candidate policy executes strictly as a feedforward computation over static sensor buffers. Because the physical environment cannot respond to emitted actions, the state sequence remains fixed to the exact trajectory recorded during prior data collection. This regime provides solid empirical evidence for computational efficiency, dynamic memory allocation, and loss metrics against a reference benchmark. It can verify, for example, whether neural network inference fits within its target execution budget on an edge accelerator, and whether output distributions align numerically with logged human demonstrations. However, recorded replay cannot substantiate any claim regarding closed-loop stability or control authority. Because predicted actions never feed back into subsequent sensor frames, errors never induce consequences: if the policy commands an aggressive steering angle, the subsequent logged frame still shows the mobile base tracking straight down the corridor.

Closed-loop simulation restores the causal feedback path by substituting an explicit mathematical or numerical model, $\SimulatedPlantDynamics$, for the physical robot and its operating environment. When the policy emits an action and the modeled safety permission path selects the control command $\AdmittedControlCommand_t$, the physics engine numerically integrates the equations of motion, advances the scene geometry, and renders synthetic sensor observations for timestep $\ControlStepIndex+1$. This regime enables exhaustive testing of closed-loop dynamics, kinematic reachability, and recovery maneuvers. It can demonstrate, for example, whether a mobile base recovers gracefully from an initial tracking offset, or whether an articulated arm avoids self-collision throughout its reachable workspace across thousands of parallelized instances. However, the resulting evidence applies exclusively to the synthetic operator $\SimulatedPlantDynamics$. Unmodeled transmission backlash\index{Mechanical backlash}, tire deformation, dynamic contact friction\index{Contact friction} transitions, and optical sensor artifacts are omitted by construction. Demonstrating stability within $\SimulatedPlantDynamics$ therefore establishes that the policy stabilizes the model, not that it will stabilize physical hardware.

Shadow operation deploys the candidate policy directly onto an active physical machine while a validated baseline controller, or a human operator, retains exclusive authority over the physical actuators. The candidate policy ingests live streaming sensor data, executes onboard inference amid real mechanical vibrations and fieldbus contention, and computes candidate actions $\CandidatePolicyAction$.[^fn-hw-hil-bus] These proposed actions are logged to high-speed storage but never dispatched to the motor drives. Shadow operation yields robust empirical proof regarding real-time system performance. It can confirm, for instance, whether the latch policy maintains its target `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_rate_str` chunk rate under sustained thermal throttling, and quantify how frequently $\CandidatePolicyAction$ deviates from the baseline control action $\BaselineControllerAction$ beyond an acceptable safety threshold.

Nevertheless, shadow operation is fundamentally limited by the **trajectory confinement problem**: because the baseline controller exercises exclusive control over the actuators, the physical robot traces trajectories governed strictly by the baseline state distribution $\BaselineStateDistribution$. If the candidate policy generates an action that would cause the arm to jam the latch, veer off course, or strike a support strut, the physical plant never executes the command. The candidate's sensory stream remains perpetually confined to the safe states visited by the baseline supervisor. As a result, shadow testing cannot reveal whether the candidate could recover from an unvisited off-nominal state, nor can it expose whether its divergent actions would have resulted in catastrophic mechanical damage.

[^fn-hw-hil-bus]: **Bus Jitter in Shadow Mode**\index{Shadow mode deployment!bus jitter}: Inference that is steady on a bench stretches on the machine when direct memory access (DMA) transfers, shared memory, and fieldbus arbitration compete for the same paths. Shadow operation logs that jitter on the real buses, under real thermal load, without letting the late proposals move the chassis.

Constrained physical testing closes the causal feedback loop on actual hardware by routing candidate policy proposals through the permission path to the actuators, strictly within an enforced safety envelope. These operational boundaries are enforced via hardware tethers, software velocity clamps, geofenced test enclosures, or a dedicated real-time permission path that intercepts and overrides unsafe setpoints with deterministic latency. Constrained testing delivers authentic empirical evidence regarding real-world contact mechanics, friction transitions, structural compliance, and sensor noise under actual operating loads, which is why the experimental door-latch trials belong in this regime.

When the safety system triggers an intervention, it alters or truncates the raw policy trajectory (${\TrialInterventionCount}_i \ge 1, \UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = 0$), leaving the candidate's unmitigated behavior permanently unobserved. Such a run answers two different questions, and the record must keep them apart. For the autonomy outcome it is an unambiguous failure, $\UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = 0$, because the candidate policy could not finish without external override; even if the supervisor guides the robot to successful task completion, the trial cannot be scored as an autonomous success. For the separate event of an unassisted crash, the question of whether the policy would have damaged something had nobody stepped in, the run is right-censored:[^fn-right-censoring-survival] the intervention terminated the trial before that terminal state could manifest, so the observation confirms neither unassisted success nor an inevitable crash. Any rigorous evaluation must report completion rates, intervention frequencies, and post-intervention recoveries strictly inside the verified operating envelope. Conflating safety-supervised task completion with unassisted policy survival commits the **censored trial fallacy**\index{Censored trial fallacy!definition}, which attributes to the machine learning policy a level of robustness that was entirely provided by the permission path or the safety operator.

[^fn-right-censoring-survival]: **Right Censoring**\index{Right censoring!intercepted runs}: In clinical survival analysis, a patient who departs a study before the terminal endpoint has an unknown time of death rather than an established long life. @kaplan1958nonparametric formalized an estimator that tracks such subjects within the population at risk only while they remain actively observed. An intercepted robotic trial is right-censored under identical logic: the intervention proves that the policy required supervisor takeover, not that the robot would have stabilized itself had the supervisor remained passive.

Certain software properties transfer cleanly across regime boundaries when inputs and execution semantics match. Deterministic numerical calculations, floating-point arithmetic invariants, and tensor shape contracts can be checked under the same precision, rounding, and overflow rules; an activation overflow transfers only when the simulator and target implement the same arithmetic behavior. In contrast, runtime execution latency, bus contention, and memory bandwidth utilization cannot transfer purely across regimes; they require re-measurement under the actual scheduling, fieldbus, and thermal environments of the deployment hardware. Above all, the operating state distribution never transfers directly. The instant the environmental operator transitions from synthetic simulation $\SimulatedPlantDynamics$ to live physical dynamics $\PhysicalPlantDynamics$, or when the arbitration parameters of the runtime permission path change, the state trajectory $\MechanicalPlantState_0, \MechanicalPlantState_1, \dots, \MechanicalPlantState_t$ rapidly diverges.

Conceptualizing these four regimes as a monotonic ladder of fidelity is a dangerous systems trap. Transitioning across replay, simulation, shadow execution, and constrained testing does not simply increase fidelity; every step exchanges one systemic distortion for another. Simulation secures closed-loop causality at the expense of authentic contact physics and sensory noise. Shadow execution reclaims real physical sensing and bus timing but surrenders candidate closed-loop causality. Constrained physical testing restores both causality and physical grounding, yet it systematically censors the state space beyond its safety boundary. Observing zero supervisor interventions across one hundred constrained trials proves that the policy maintained states within the un-triggered safety envelope; it offers no statistical guarantee about how the policy behaves once it breaches that boundary.

System verification therefore demands assigning each engineering question to the specific regime equipped to answer it (@tbl-07-evidence-regimes). For the latch manipulation policy, verifying whether chunk inference executes reliably within its allocated cycle time belongs first in recorded replay and subsequently in hardware shadow mode; testing whether the manipulator can recover from a wide range of positional offsets belongs in high-throughput simulation, where thousands of permutations inflict zero hardware wear; and evaluating whether passive gripper compliance and contact friction remain within structural force limits belongs strictly in constrained physical trials. Each regime remains blind to the failure modes of the others.

| Evaluation Evidence Regime       | Causal Feedback Coupling                                                                                                  | Physical Realism                                          | Supported Empirical Evidence                            | Masked Failure Mode / Boundary Distortion                                                 |
|:---------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Recorded Replay**              | Open Loop ($\partial \MechanicalPlantState_{t+1}/\partial \PredictedPolicyAction_t = \ZeroVector$)                        | Static Demonstration Buffers $\DemonstrationDataset$      | Latency budget, DRAM footprint, numerical accuracy      | Covariate shift; errors never alter subsequent observations                               |
| **Closed-Loop Simulation**       | Closed Loop ($\MechanicalPlantState_{t+1} = \SimulatedPlantDynamics(\MechanicalPlantState_t, \AdmittedControlCommand_t)$) | Synthetic Physics Operator $\SimulatedPlantDynamics$      | Kinematic reachability, large parallel test suites      | Sim-to-real gap; unmodeled contact non-linearities and tire slip                          |
| **Shadow Mode Operation**        | Open Loop for candidate (actions muted)                                                                                   | Physical machine $\PhysicalPlantDynamics$                 | Bus contention, thermal throttling, real sensor noise   | Trajectory confinement; states locked to baseline controller $\BaselineStateDistribution$ |
| **Constrained Physical Testing** | Closed Loop with permission-path override ($\SafeOverrideCommand$)                                                        | Physical machine $\PhysicalPlantDynamics$ within envelope | Contact dynamics, compliance, friction, actuator limits | State censorship; permission-path overrides and tethers truncate failure tails            |

: **Evaluation evidence regimes compared**: Trade-offs between causal feedback coupling, environmental realism, supported empirical claims, and experimental boundary distortions across the four testing regimes. No single environment evaluates open deployment; rigorous certification requires combining complementary regimes rather than assuming a linear fidelity ladder. {#tbl-07-evidence-regimes tbl-colwidths="[20,20,20,20,20]"}

### Simulation as a conditional proxy {#sec-evaluation-proxy-transfer-law}

A simulator can effectively screen candidate latch policies before committing expensive hardware to physical trials, but its screening validity depends strictly on how accurately it models the physical mechanisms governing the decision. The paired probes developed in @sec-training-contact-exploit drive the simulated and physical strike plates with identical commands and measure their discrepancies in newtons and milliseconds. The evaluation protocol incorporates those measured discrepancies directly into its test plan: while a favorable simulated recovery qualifies a checkpoint for physical verification, that result cannot resolve unmodeled discrepancies in the contact physics or data transport pipeline. Visual rendering artifacts, numerical friction regularization, and absent force-torque feedback can each alter candidate policy rankings.

Whether a simulator ranks candidate policies correctly is an empirical, measurable property. Proxy fidelity is measured with a paired benchmark across both regimes, which evaluates the same set of candidate policies (such as the latch training checkpoints) on both the simulated door mechanism and the physical hardware under tightly matched initial conditions and compares the resulting performance orderings. While a standard Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficient between simulated and physical success rates summarizes overall monotonic agreement, correlation alone can hide catastrophic failure modes. Specifically, a high correlation coefficient can easily coexist with a critical rank inversion, in which the simulator mistakenly promotes a checkpoint that fails dangerously when deployed on the physical door. To address this risk, @li2024simpler measure rank agreement with the mean maximum rank violation (MMRV), computed across approximately 1,500 paired simulated and physical episodes. For each policy, MMRV finds its worst inversion against any other policy, weighting each pair the simulator orders wrongly by the two policies' real-world performance gap, and then averages those worst cases across policies, so a simulator scores badly exactly when it swaps policies whose physical performance differs most.

This evaluation principle applies directly to the latch manipulation task. A simulator whose relative rankings across historical checkpoints correlate reliably with physical trials earns the operational authority to screen incoming models. Conversely, a simulation environment that has never been calibrated against paired physical benchmarks possesses no screening credibility, regardless of how photorealistic its graphics engine appears. The identical constraint governs learned neural world models deployed as simulated environments: predicted candidate success serves as a justification for scheduling physical tests, not as verifiable evidence of physical capability, until paired real-world trials validate model calibration. Furthermore, even a validated ranking proxy only authorizes candidate filtering. Physical trials remain the ultimate ground truth for safety and performance guarantees, because knowing that policy A outperforms policy B reveals nothing about whether policy A satisfies the machine's absolute failure-rate limits.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Learned world models used as simulators, whose simplifications cannot be enumerated, are established in @sec-training-world-models.
:::

Two additional systems factors dictate the generalization bounds of any simulation-based evaluation: parameter domain coverage and execution timing fidelity.

The first factor is the physical parameter variation spanned during simulation trials. A simulation calibrated against telemetry logs from a single robotic arm provides evidence strictly for that physical unit under those specific ambient conditions. Similarly, domain randomization evaluates policy resilience only across the bounded support of the randomized parameter distributions; it cannot account for dynamic phenomena entirely absent from the simulator's underlying differential equations. Formal sim-to-real gap analysis identifies unmodeled dynamics and compiles them into the omission log that the policy manifest carries. The closed-loop evaluation protocol must incorporate that log directly, cataloging the operating regimes and edge conditions about which simulation can make no empirical claims.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Formal sim-to-real gap analysis, which yields a supported region and a residual mismatch list, is established in @sec-training-sim-to-real-gap.
:::

The second factor is whether the evaluation regime reflects true hardware execution dynamics. Standard software-in-the-loop simulations pause virtual simulation time while the policy executes neural inference, masking real-world computational bottlenecks. A simulator that pauses virtual time during inference cannot expose the consequences of a late inference chunk, a rejected stale proposal, or an executing chunk that continues under its `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` chunk lease while awaiting updated sensor verification. Explicit delay models can exercise those transitions, but establishing their actual timing requires the neural policy and runtime permission arbiter on target embedded compute hardware interconnected via the physical buses.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The chunk lease, sized between the renewal floor and the stopping budget, is established in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing.
:::

Closed-loop simulation, whether executed purely in software or integrated with hardware in the loop, serves as an indispensable filter for screening candidate models. However, only physical trials measure true embodied competence, and engineers must formalize the safety envelopes and evaluation protocols long before the first trial begins.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The qualification ladder, which stages software-, processor-, and hardware-in-the-loop benches before physical fault rigs, is developed in @sec-verification-qualification-ladder.
:::

::: {#chk-eval-evidence-regimes .callout-checkpoint title="Trade-offs across evidence regimes"}

Before fixing a physical trial protocol, review evidence regimes and fidelity trade-offs:

- [ ] **Regime causality trade-offs**: Contrast the causal feedback properties of recorded trace replay against closed-loop simulation.
- [ ] **Shadow-mode trajectory confinement**: Explain why shadow-mode evaluation on the running machine cannot test the candidate policy's recovery maneuvers.
- [ ] **Transfer across regimes**: Describe which properties transfer reliably across regimes and which one stays behind.

:::
## Fixing the Trial Protocol {#sec-evaluation-trial-protocol}

Empirical success probabilities and intervention rates are meaningful only with respect to a specific joint distribution $\OperationalTestDistribution$ over initial system states, environmental parameters, and task goals. Consequently, the intended operating region must be formalized before executing a single physical trial. The **target ODD**\index{Operational design domain!target ODD} is the concrete subset of the declared ODD recorded by the policy manifest of @sec-training-policy-manifest that the evaluation campaign samples. Its sampling weights define $\OperationalTestDistribution$, and no rigorous empirical claim reaches beyond its support. If an engineering team executes fifty ad hoc physical runs across arbitrary trajectories and reports a 90 percent success rate, that statistic lacks an interpretable denominator. A measured success rate supports a target-distribution claim only when the support and sampling weights of $\OperationalTestDistribution$ are specified in advance, establishing explicit bounds on scene illuminance, payload mass and inertia, surface friction coefficients, allowable initial state offsets, and the specific hardware serial numbers under test.

Extracting valid confidence bounds from empirical trials requires three operational conditions:

1. *Independent and identically distributed (iid) sampling:* Trials must be independent realizations drawn from $\OperationalTestDistribution$. In embodied physical systems, standard offline dataset intuition often fails; randomly shuffling log records cannot eliminate physical coupling. On real robotic hardware, thermal accumulation in motor windings from resistive heating ($\WindingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance$), battery voltage sag under discharge, and progressive mechanical backlash introduce temporal autocorrelation across sequential trials. Run 20 is not drawn from the same physical distribution as Run 1 unless operators strictly enforce thermal cooldown intervals and battery recharging cycles between runs. Furthermore, repeated trials executed on a single physical unit (such as Unit 01) cannot serve as iid draws from the broader fleet distribution $\FleetManufacturingDistribution$, because unit-level manufacturing tolerances and sensor calibrations bias the sample.
2. *Fixed outcome predicates:* The binary evaluation function $\EvaluationPredicate$ and termination criteria $\TerminationProtocol$ must remain frozen throughout the entire campaign. Modifying the execution deadline $\CompletionDeadline$, adjusting collision thresholds, or widening the spatial tolerance of goal region $\GoalSet$ midway through testing alters the definition of success. Doing so commits post-hoc metric drift and invalidates statistical comparisons against baseline models.
3. *Full-denominator accounting:* Every initiated run must remain in the evaluation ledger, including hardware communication faults, sensor timeouts, emergency protective stops, and operator interventions. Culling inconvenient or anomalous runs corrupts the statistical denominator. A hardware abort that halts execution prior to goal completion yields a task failure ($\TrialCompletionIndicator = 0$). Under a strict autonomy metric, any human intervention forces $\UnassistedSuccessIndicator = 0$; an operator nudge that guides the robot around an obstacle followed by on-time completion records $\TrialCompletionIndicator = 1$ and $\UnassistedSuccessIndicator = 0$. Safety monitoring systems must record kinematic limit violations and physical damage separately from task completion. When a safety tripwire or human supervisor intercepts an impending collision, the counterfactual unmitigated trajectory remains unknown. Consequently, zero recorded damage cannot be credited as evidence of unassisted survival. Discarding aborted or intercepted runs changes the underlying question and inflates perceived reliability by measuring an idealized survivor population.

When these conditions hold, the sample mean provides an unbiased point estimate of the policy's closed-loop performance under $\OperationalTestDistribution$. The remaining engineering challenge is determining how much statistical uncertainty a finite sample leaves, particularly when high-reliability targets yield zero observed failures across the test budget.

## Confidence from a Finite Campaign {#sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-clopper-pearson-zero-failure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOPPER-PEARSON ZERO-FAILURE RELIABILITY SIZING (LEGO)

# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound, @sec-evaluation-logs, and the takeaways.
# │ Show: One-sided confidence limits for iid zero-failure trials, not a rate estimate.
# │ How: p_lower = alpha^(1/n); failure_upper = 1 - p_lower.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt_int, fmt, check, MarkdownStr

class ClopperPearsonZeroFailure:
    """Exact binomial confidence bounds for physical robotics qualification."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_runs = 20  # category: illustrative; the opening campaign's clean runs
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    alpha = 1.0 - confidence  # category: derived; significance level
    n_one_in = 8  # category: illustrative; a policy that fails one run in eight
    n_fallacy = 1000  # category: illustrative; clean openings in the perfect-record fallacy
    n_looks = 5  # category: illustrative; independent 5 percent looks in the optional-stopping example

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_lower = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_runs, confidence=confidence)
    failure_upper = 1.0 - p_lower
    p_clean_one_in = (1.0 - 1.0 / n_one_in) ** n_runs  # chance that policy still logs n_runs clean runs

    p_clean_at_bound = p_lower**n_runs  # probability of n clean runs at the bound itself; equals alpha

    # Scaling to 90, 99, and 99.9% reliability
    p_target_90 = 0.90  # category: chosen; pilot target in the fallacy and the SPRT contrast
    p_target_99 = 0.99  # category: chosen; industrial target in the prose
    p_target_999 = 0.999  # category: chosen; the target the chapter argues toward
    n_req_90 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target_90, confidence=confidence)
    n_req_99 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target_99, confidence=confidence)
    n_req_999 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target_999, confidence=confidence)
    rule_of_three_20 = 3.0 / n_runs  # Rule of Three approximation to failure_upper at n_runs
    n_cells_joint = 2  # category: illustrative; nominal and displaced-plate cells of the recovery branch
    n_req_999_joint = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target_999, confidence=1.0 - alpha / n_cells_joint)  # Bonferroni split
    p_lower_fallacy = calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_fallacy, confidence=confidence)
    p_any_false_positive = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) ** n_looks  # chance of at least one false positive across independent looks
    ln_inv_alpha = math.log(1.0 / alpha)  # the numerator of every zero-failure count; about 3 at 95 percent
    ln_inv_alpha_per_run = ln_inv_alpha / n_runs  # exponent of the 20-run bound, shown in the notebook
    ln_inv_999 = -math.log(p_target_999)  # per-run log cost of a 99.9 percent target, shown in the notebook
    p_target_chk = 0.995  # category: chosen; target in the bounds checkpoint's budget estimate

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(p_lower - 0.8609) < 0.001, "Unexpected 20-run lower bound")
    check(abs(failure_upper - 0.1391) < 0.001, "Unexpected 20-run upper confidence limit")
    check(n_req_999 == 2995, "Unexpected sample size for 99.9% reliability")
    check(n_req_999_joint == 3688, "Splitting alpha over two cells should need 3,688 runs per cell")
    check(n_req_99 == 299 and n_req_90 == 29, "Zero-failure counts for 99 and 90 percent should be 299 and 29")
    check(abs(p_clean_at_bound - alpha) < 1e-12, "At the lower bound, n clean runs must have probability alpha")
    check(p_clean_one_in > alpha, "The one-in-eight policy must pass 20/20 more often than alpha")
    check(n_one_in == 8 and abs(p_clean_one_in - 0.0692) < 0.001, "Unexpected clean-record probability for a one-in-eight policy")
    check(p_lower_fallacy < p_target_999 and abs(p_lower_fallacy - 0.9970) < 0.0001, "The 1,000-run bound must fall short of 99.9 percent")
    check(abs(p_any_false_positive - 0.2262) < 0.001, "Five independent 5 percent looks should give about 22.6 percent")
    check(abs(math.exp(-ln_inv_alpha_per_run) - p_lower) < 1e-12, "Notebook arithmetic must reproduce the 20-run bound")
    check(math.ceil(ln_inv_alpha / ln_inv_999) == n_req_999, "Notebook arithmetic must reproduce 2,995 runs")
    check(rule_of_three_20 > failure_upper, "The Rule of Three overstates the exact limit at n = 20")
    # margin_nonasymptotic_reliability_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 20, 29, 299, 2,995 runs and 86.1 percent
    check(n_runs == 20 and f"{100 * p_lower:.1f}" == "86.1", "Ladder fig-alt states 20 runs at 86.1 percent")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_runs_str = fmt_int(n_runs)
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_lower_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_lower, precision=1, style="prose")
    failure_upper_pct_str = fmt_percent(failure_upper, precision=1, style="prose")
    p_lower_val_str = fmt(p_lower, precision=3)
    n_req_999_str = fmt_int(n_req_999, commas=True)
    n_req_99_str = fmt_int(n_req_99, commas=True)
    n_req_999_joint_str = fmt_int(n_req_999_joint, commas=True)
    alpha_joint_str = fmt(alpha / n_cells_joint, precision=3)
    n_req_90_str = fmt_int(n_req_90)
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha, precision=2)
    p_one_in_str = fmt(1.0 - 1.0 / n_one_in, precision=3)
    rule_of_three_20_str = fmt(rule_of_three_20, precision=2)
    _words = {5: "five", 8: "eight"}
    n_one_in_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_one_in])
    p_clean_one_in_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_clean_one_in, precision=1, style="prose")
    n_fallacy_str = fmt_int(n_fallacy, commas=True)
    p_lower_fallacy_str = fmt(p_lower_fallacy, precision=4)
    n_looks_str = MarkdownStr(_words[n_looks].capitalize())
    p_any_false_positive_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_any_false_positive, precision=1, style="prose")
    ln_inv_alpha_str = fmt(ln_inv_alpha, precision=3)
    one_in_upper_str = MarkdownStr({7: "seven"}[round(1.0 / failure_upper)])
    ln_inv_alpha_per_run_str = fmt(ln_inv_alpha_per_run, precision=4)
    ln_inv_999_str = fmt(ln_inv_999, precision=7)
    p_target_999_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_target_999, precision=1, style="prose")
    p_target_chk_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_target_chk, precision=1, style="prose")
```

With the operational outcome, target population, evaluation regime, and trial denominator fixed, the twenty clean nominal runs pose an immediate statistical problem: determining what degree of reliability the campaign has actually demonstrated. A confidence bound quantifies the uncertainty that remains under the declared sampling model. Systems engineers must treat this bound as a measure of statistical evidence rather than an assessment of physical failure severity or an automatic deployment permit.

The standard textbook interval for a proportion, the Wald normal approximation $\ObservedSuccessFraction \pm 1.96\sqrt{\ObservedSuccessFraction(1-\ObservedSuccessFraction)/\TrialCount}$, collapses to zero width when the observed success fraction $\ObservedSuccessFraction$ reaches 1.0 because its sample variance term vanishes. This collapse exposes the complete breakdown of the asymptotic normal assumption near the boundary rather than empirical certainty. Evaluating the statistical assurance of a zero-failure record requires only the product rule for independent events.

Suppose the true per-run success probability of the latch policy is $\TrialSuccessProbability$. If individual trials are independent, twenty consecutive runs all succeed with joint probability $\TrialSuccessProbability^{20}$. Consider a flawed policy that fails one run in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_one_in_str` ($\TrialSuccessProbability =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_one_in_str`). That policy still produces an unbroken twenty-run success streak in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in_pct_str` of evaluation campaigns; an empirical run of twenty successes cannot rule it out. As the candidate success rate $\TrialSuccessProbability$ decreases, a clean record becomes increasingly improbable. When $\TrialSuccessProbability$ drops to `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str`, the probability of observing twenty consecutive successes falls to exactly $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str`, which corresponds to the significance level for a 95 percent confidence requirement ($1 - 0.95$). Any underlying success probability lower than `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str` would make the observed twenty-run clean record rarer than a 1-in-20 chance ($\TrialSuccessProbability^{20} < 0.05$). The one-sided lower confidence bound therefore identifies the threshold below which candidate policies become statistically inconsistent with the experimental data. In standard frequentist qualification, "95 percent confidence" describes the long-run coverage of the testing protocol: across repeated qualification campaigns, the procedure traps the true parameter $\TrialSuccessProbability$ above the calculated bound at least 95 percent of the time. The bound represents a conservative floor under the declared sampling model rather than a point estimate of $\TrialSuccessProbability$ or a Bayesian posterior belief about this specific policy.

Reading the inversion as a curve makes the logic visible. Plotting $\TrialSuccessProbability^{20}$ against every candidate $\TrialSuccessProbability$ (@fig-07-clean-run-inversion) shows the clean record ruling out only the candidates whose curve lies below the $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$ line, the region left of $\TrialSuccessProbability =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str`. The one-in-eight policy sits just above that line, which is why twenty flawless runs cannot reject it.

::: {#fig-07-clean-run-inversion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Inverting a clean record into a bound**: The probability that `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` independent runs all succeed, $\TrialSuccessProbability^{20}$, against the true per-run success probability $\TrialSuccessProbability$. Candidates left of the crossing with $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str` would make the observed record rarer than one campaign in twenty, so the record rules them out; the crossing at $\TrialSuccessProbability =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str` is the lower bound. The one-in-eight policy still logs a clean record in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in_pct_str` of campaigns." fig-alt="Log-scale plot of the probability of twenty clean runs against the true success probability from 0.70 to 1.00. The rising curve crosses a horizontal dashed line at 0.05 near a success probability of 0.861, marked with a dot and a vertical dropline; the region left of the crossing is shaded gray. A second marker at a success probability of 0.875 sits slightly above the line at about 0.069."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLEAN-RECORD PROBABILITY AND ITS INVERSION (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-07-clean-run-inversion
# │ Goal:    show what the one-sided lower bound is before any formula
# │ Show:    P(n clean runs | p) = p**n, the alpha line, the crossing at
# │          p_lower, and the one-in-eight policy above the line
# │ How:     every plotted value is read from ClopperPearsonZeroFailure
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4))

# ┌── 1. LOAD (from the LEGO cell) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
CP = ClopperPearsonZeroFailure
n_runs = CP.n_runs
alpha = CP.alpha
p_lower = CP.p_lower
p_one_in = 1.0 - 1.0 / CP.n_one_in
p_clean_one_in = CP.p_clean_one_in

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
p = np.linspace(0.70, 1.0, 600)
p_clean = p**n_runs
check(abs(p_lower**n_runs - alpha) < 1e-12, "The crossing must sit on the alpha line")

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
y_min = 5e-4
ax.axvspan(0.70, p_lower, color=COLORS["grid"], alpha=0.25, lw=0)
ax.plot(p, p_clean, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.0)
ax.axhline(alpha, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=1.0, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
ax.text(0.705, alpha * 1.12, f"$\\alpha_{{\\mathrm{{sig}}}}$ = {alpha:.2f}", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["primary"], va="bottom")
ax.text(0.705, 0.6, f"ruled out by {n_runs} clean runs", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["primary"], va="center")

ax.plot([p_lower, p_lower], [y_min, alpha], color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9)
ax.plot([p_lower], [alpha], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"lower bound\np = {p_lower:.3f}",
    xy=(p_lower, alpha),
    xytext=(0.80, 0.25),
    fontsize=9,
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, shrinkB=5),
)
ax.plot([p_one_in], [p_clean_one_in], "s", ms=6, mfc="white", mec=COLORS["primary"], mew=1.3, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"fails one run in {CP.n_one_in}\np = {p_one_in:.3f}, clean {p_clean_one_in:.1%}",
    xy=(p_one_in, p_clean_one_in),
    xytext=(0.915, 8e-3),
    fontsize=9,
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, shrinkB=5),
)

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.70, 1.0)
ax.set_ylim(y_min, 1.3)
ax.set_xlabel("True per-run success probability p")
ax.set_ylabel(f"P({n_runs} clean runs) = $p^{{{n_runs}}}$ (log scale)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

For a predeclared zero-failure campaign of $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ trials, this inversion yields the exact one-sided Clopper-Pearson lower bound\index{Clopper-Pearson non-asymptotic bound!definition}\index{Clopper-Pearson method}[^fn-clopper-pearson-exact] [@clopper1934use]. Setting $\TrialSuccessProbability^\ZeroFailureTrialCount = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$ gives
$$\SuccessLowerConfidenceLimit = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel^{1/\ZeroFailureTrialCount}$$ {#eq-eval-zero-failure-bound}
with the corresponding upper confidence limit on the per-run failure probability given by:
$$\FailureUpperConfidenceLimit = 1 - \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel^{1/\ZeroFailureTrialCount}$$
@Sec-evaluation-bounds-with-failures extends this inversion principle to evaluation campaigns that record failures.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The discrete and continuous-time derivations of the zero-failure bound, and why the normal approximation fails at zero failures, are developed in @sec-appendix-ml-exposure.
:::

[^fn-clopper-pearson-exact]: **Exact Binomial Bound**\index{Clopper-Pearson method!exact inversion}: @clopper1934use inverted the binomial tail directly instead of approximating it with a normal distribution. Here "exact" denotes that algebraic inversion rather than exact coverage probability; because binomial counts are discrete, the true coverage equals or exceeds the nominal confidence level for all values of $\TrialSuccessProbability$. Under the declared binomial sampling model, the procedure places the lower bound at or below the true reliability in at least the nominal fraction of repeated campaigns; an individual campaign can still overstate it.

For rare failures ($\TrialFailureProbability \ll 1$), a first-order Taylor series expansion linearizes this bound into the **rule of three**\index{Rule of three!definition} [@hanley1983nothing]. Expanding $\ln(1 - \TrialFailureProbability) = -\TrialFailureProbability - \TrialFailureProbability^2/2 - \dots \approx -\TrialFailureProbability$ and setting the clean-run probability $(1 - \TrialFailureProbability)^\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ equal to $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel = 0.05$ yields $-\ZeroFailureTrialCount\,\TrialFailureProbability \approx \ln(0.05) \approx -2.996 \approx -3.0$. When $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ independent trials pass without a single failure, the upper 95 percent confidence limit on the per-trial failure probability simplifies to:
$$\ZeroFailureUpperConfidenceLimit \approx \frac{3}{\ZeroFailureTrialCount}.$$ {#eq-eval-rule-of-three}
Inverted to size test campaigns, the rule establishes the empirical burden for any target reliability: $\ZeroFailureTrialCount \approx 3 / (1 - \TargetTrialSuccessProbability)$. Each additional "nine" of target reliability multiplies the required trial volume tenfold. For the twenty door-opening trials, @eq-eval-rule-of-three yields an approximate upper failure bound of $3/20 =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.rule_of_three_20_str`, whereas the exact Clopper-Pearson computation in notebook \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} establishes `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str`. A policy with a true failure probability as high as `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` remains entirely compatible with twenty consecutive successes at 95 percent confidence. The campaign cannot substantiate an industrial claim of 99 percent reliability. Formally certifying a 99 percent lower confidence limit ($\TargetTrialSuccessProbability = 0.99$) at 95 percent confidence demands:
$$\ZeroFailureTrialCount = \left\lceil \frac{\ln(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel)}{\ln(\TargetTrialSuccessProbability)} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.99)} \right\rceil$$ {#eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size}
which equals `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_99_str` consecutive clean trials, an order of magnitude beyond the twenty trials conducted in the initial campaign.[^fn-math-rule-three]

The bound inherits the iid condition of @sec-evaluation-trial-protocol. Twenty runs on Unit 01 therefore bound Unit 01's success probability under the sampled conditions and nothing more; the unit-to-unit variance of @sec-evaluation-what-measured puts Unit 02 in a different population, whose bound needs its own trials or a sample drawn across the fleet.

[^fn-math-rule-three]: **Rule of Three**\index{Rule of three!clinical origin}: The heuristic originates in biostatistics, where @hanley1983nothing evaluated the risk to future patients following a clinical trial with zero adverse events across $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ participants. An embodied evaluation campaign asks an identical question of the next robot trial, and the same $3/\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ ratio governs the bound.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_nonasymptotic_reliability_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar ladder on a log scale of consecutive clean runs and the 95 percent success lower limit each supports: 20 runs give 86.1 percent, 29 runs give 90 percent, 299 runs give 99 percent, and 2,995 runs give 99.9 percent."}
*Each added nine of reliability costs ten times the clean runs.*
:::

::: {#nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound .callout-notebook title="The clean-record bound"}

**Problem**: The mobile manipulator completes $\ZeroFailureTrialCount =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` door-opening runs with no contact-tripwire crossing and no intervention. What one-sided `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.confidence_pct_str` lower limit on its per-run success probability $\TrialSuccessProbability$ does that record support, and what does it cost to claim `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_target_999_pct_str` instead?

**Variables**:

* $\ZeroFailureTrialCount =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` clean runs (Illustrative; the chapter's opening campaign, independent and identically distributed draws from the target operational design domain).
* $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str` (Chosen; one minus the 95 percent confidence level).

**Math**: Setting $\TrialSuccessProbability^{\ZeroFailureTrialCount} = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$ (@eq-eval-zero-failure-bound) and taking logarithms, $\ln(1/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel) =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.ln_inv_alpha_str`, divided by $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ gives the exponent `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.ln_inv_alpha_per_run_str`, and $\SuccessLowerConfidenceLimit$ is $\Glyph{e}$ raised to minus that exponent, `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str`. The failure upper limit is $1 - \SuccessLowerConfidenceLimit$, or `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str`, which the rule of three (@eq-eval-rule-of-three) approximates as $3/20 =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.rule_of_three_20_str`.

**Result**: `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` success lower limit at 95 percent confidence; a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_target_999_pct_str` limit needs `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` clean runs (notebook \ref{nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance}).

**Systems insight**: Twenty clean runs leave a failure probability as high as one run in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.one_in_upper_str` statistically consistent with the empirical data. The evaluation campaign establishes a formal lower confidence bound under its specific sampling assumptions; it should never be conflated with a steady-state failure rate, an MTBF, or an unconditional deployment authorization. Improving the bound requires scaling $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$, because the numerator $\ln(1/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel) \approx 3$ remains anchored by the chosen confidence level. This structural property explains why the rule of three matches the exact Clopper-Pearson bound whenever failure probabilities are small.

:::

### Bounds when failures occur {#sec-evaluation-bounds-with-failures}

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-bound-with-failures
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE-SIDED CLOPPER-PEARSON LOWER BOUND WITH FAILURES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-bounds-with-failures.
# │ Show: the 95 percent lower bound when a twenty-run campaign has one failure,
# │       beside the zero-failure bound.
# │ How: solve P(X >= k | n, p) = alpha for p by bisection, X ~ Binomial(n, p);
# │      at k = n this reduces to p^n = alpha (the zero-failure case).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, check

def _binom_upper_tail(k, n, p):
    """P(X >= k) for X ~ Binomial(n, p)."""
    return sum(math.comb(n, j) * p**j * (1.0 - p) ** (n - j) for j in range(k, n + 1))

def _cp_lower(k, n, alpha):
    """One-sided Clopper-Pearson lower limit on p after k successes in n trials."""
    if k == 0:
        return 0.0
    lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        if _binom_upper_tail(k, n, mid) > alpha:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)

class BoundWithFailures:
    """Lower confidence bound for a campaign that records failures."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_runs = ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs  # category: illustrative; the opening campaign size
    n_fail = 1  # category: illustrative; one failed run in the same campaign
    alpha = ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha  # category: chosen; one-sided significance level

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    k_success = n_runs - n_fail
    p_lower_one_fail = _cp_lower(k_success, n_runs, alpha)
    p_lower_zero_fail = _cp_lower(n_runs, n_runs, alpha)
    p_hat = k_success / n_runs

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(p_lower_zero_fail - ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower) < 1e-9, "k = n must reproduce alpha^(1/n)")
    check(abs(p_lower_one_fail - 0.7839) < 0.0005, "19 of 20 should give a 95 percent lower bound near 78.4 percent")
    check(p_lower_one_fail < p_lower_zero_fail < 1.0, "A failure must lower the bound")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    p_hat_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_hat, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_lower_one_fail_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_lower_one_fail, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Encountering an operational failure during testing does not invalidate statistical evaluation; rather, it shifts the calculation from a zero-failure boundary to the full binomial distribution. Given $\SuccessfulTrialCount$ successful trials out of $\TrialCount$ total runs, the one-sided lower confidence limit is the parameter value $\TrialSuccessProbability$ for which the probability of observing $\SuccessfulTrialCount$ or more successes equals $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$:
$$\Pr(\BinomialSuccessCount \ge \SuccessfulTrialCount \mid \TrialCount, \TrialSuccessProbability) = \sum_{\SuccessCountIndex=\SuccessfulTrialCount}^{\TrialCount} \binom{\TrialCount}{\SuccessCountIndex} \TrialSuccessProbability^{\SuccessCountIndex} (1-\TrialSuccessProbability)^{\TrialCount-\SuccessCountIndex} = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel,$$ {#eq-eval-bound-with-failures}
where the random variable $\BinomialSuccessCount$ denotes the success count. When $\SuccessfulTrialCount = \TrialCount$, the summation collapses to a single term, $\TrialSuccessProbability^\TrialCount = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$, recovering the zero-failure Clopper-Pearson bound of @eq-eval-zero-failure-bound. If the mobile manipulator logs a single failure across twenty runs ($\SuccessfulTrialCount = 19$), the relationship expands to $\TrialSuccessProbability^{20} + 20\,\TrialSuccessProbability^{19}(1-\TrialSuccessProbability) = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$. Although this polynomial lacks a closed-form algebraic root, numerical root-finding yields a 95 percent lower confidence limit of `{python} BoundWithFailures.p_lower_one_fail_pct_str`. Even though the empirical success fraction is `{python} BoundWithFailures.p_hat_pct_str`, a single observed failure drops the certified lower bound from `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` to `{python} BoundWithFailures.p_lower_one_fail_pct_str`. In production evaluation pipelines, libraries compute this limit directly using quantiles of the incomplete beta function, exploiting the exact mathematical identity between binomial tails and Beta distributions.

Two critical engineering cautions govern this methodology. First, any observed failure must remain permanently logged in the audit trail. Halting a test campaign upon observing an anomaly and restarting a clean run counter introduces severe optional-stopping bias; engineers cannot subsequently claim a zero-failure bound on the post-restart run sequence (@sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim). Second, the Clopper-Pearson method is conservative by construction because its coverage probability equals or exceeds the nominal confidence level for every value of $\TrialSuccessProbability$. For standard exploratory data analysis, @brown2001interval recommend the Wilson score interval[^fn-wilson-score-interval] or Jeffreys prior intervals, which maintain average coverage closer to nominal while producing tighter intervals. For physical qualification and safety certification, however, overestimating autonomous reliability is the catastrophic failure mode. The conservative Clopper-Pearson bound therefore serves as the defensible systems default, and engineering test records must explicitly state the inference method applied.

[^fn-wilson-score-interval]: **Wilson Interval**\index{Wilson interval!zero-failure records}: @wilson1927probable inverted the score test around the parameter $\TrialSuccessProbability$ rather than substituting the empirical estimator $\ObservedSuccessFraction$, allowing the interval to maintain a nonzero width even when $\ObservedSuccessFraction = 1.0$. This formulation resolves the boundary collapse of the Wald normal approximation. However, because its coverage guarantees hold on average across the parameter space rather than strictly at every point $\TrialSuccessProbability$, physical qualification protocols default to the exact Clopper-Pearson bound.

The twenty nominal door-opening runs now have a concrete statistical interpretation under non-asymptotic sampling theory. Elevating the certified lower bound requires systematically expanding the trial budget, directly compounding the physical testing hours, mechanical wear, and facility costs necessary to qualify embodied machine learning policies.

## Trial Budgets, Stopping Rules, and Comparisons {#sec-evaluation-trial-limits}

Every reliability claim is paid for in physical trials. Statistical theory dictates how many trials a claim demands, but on a physical machine the plant, not the compute budget, determines what each trial costs. While a million software unit tests consume only processor cycles, each closed-loop trial of a physical robot consumes test-cell time, exhausts bearing and linkage fatigue life, burns thermal headroom in motor windings, and risks costly hardware damage. Sizing a qualification campaign therefore means reconciling the trial count required by statistical confidence with the operational time and fatigue life of the testbed that must supply it. That disciplined reconciliation separates a rigorous qualification argument from an anecdotal demonstration. The same budget pressure then motivates the two refinements that close the section: stopping a campaign early without inflating its error rates, and deciding whether a retrained checkpoint is better than the one it would replace.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-door-cycle
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WALL-CLOCK COST OF THE DOOR CAMPAIGN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-evaluation-trial-limits, @nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance,
# │          @fig-07-confidence-bounds, and @tbl-07-confidence-bounds.
# │ Show: one door trial's test-cell time (run plus reset) and what the
# │       opening campaign and a 99.9 percent campaign occupy at that cycle.
# │ How: T_cycle = t_run + t_reset; T_campaign = n * T_cycle, with n from
# │      calc_zero_failure_sample_size.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_time, fmt_int, check, MarkdownStr

class DoorCycle:
    """Test-cell time per door trial and per zero-failure campaign."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_run = 25.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; drive-in from the standoff, stop, guarded unlatch and swing
    t_reset = 15.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; re-latch, return to the standoff, telemetry flush
    n_opening = 20  # category: illustrative; the opening campaign's clean runs
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    p_target = 0.999  # category: chosen; success lower limit the section argues toward
    n_operators = 2  # category: illustrative; safety operators watching each run
    table_n = (10, 20, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2995)  # category: chosen; rows of @tbl-07-confidence-bounds

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_cycle = (t_run + t_reset).to(ureg.second)
    n_target = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(p_target, confidence=confidence)
    t_opening = (n_opening * t_cycle).to(minute)
    t_target = (n_target * t_cycle).to(ureg.hour)
    t_target_days = t_target.to(ureg.day)
    t_target_operator = t_target * n_operators
    shifts_target = (t_target_operator / (8.0 * ureg.hour)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    table_hours = [n * c for n, c in zip(table_n, [t_cycle.to(ureg.hour)] * len(table_n))]  # zip: class scope is not visible inside the comprehension

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_cycle.to(ureg.second).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Door cycle should be 40 s")
    check(t_run == JamReset.t_run, "The door run must match the jammed-reset example")
    check(n_target == 2995, "Zero-failure trials for a 99.9 percent lower limit should be 2,995")
    check(abs(t_opening.to(minute).magnitude - 13.33) < 0.005, "Twenty runs should take about 13.3 min")
    check(abs(t_target.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 33.28) < 0.005, "2,995 runs should take about 33.3 h")
    check(abs(t_target_operator.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 66.56) < 0.01, "Two operators should spend about 66.6 h")
    check(8 < shifts_target < 9, "Prose says over eight eight-hour shifts")
    check(table_n[-1] == n_target, "Last table row must be the 99.9 percent sample size")
    check(abs((n_target * t_cycle).to(ureg.second).magnitude - 119800) < 1e-6, "Notebook shows 2,995 x 40 s = 119,800 s")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_run_str = fmt_time(t_run, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_reset_str = fmt_time(t_reset, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_cycle_str = fmt_time(t_cycle, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_opening_str = fmt_time(t_opening, unit=minute, precision=1)
    t_target_str = fmt_time(t_target, unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    t_target_s_str = fmt_time((n_target * t_cycle).to(ureg.second), unit=ureg.second, precision=0, commas=True)
    t_target_days_str = fmt_time(t_target_days, unit=ureg.day, precision=1, style="word")
    t_target_operator_str = fmt_time(t_target_operator, unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    shifts_floor_str = MarkdownStr({8: "eight", 9: "nine"}[int(shifts_target)])
    n_operators_str = MarkdownStr({2: "two", 3: "three"}[n_operators])
    h_10_str = fmt_time(table_hours[0], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_20_str = fmt_time(table_hours[1], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_50_str = fmt_time(table_hours[2], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_100_str = fmt_time(table_hours[3], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_250_str = fmt_time(table_hours[4], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_500_str = fmt_time(table_hours[5], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_1000_str = fmt_time(table_hours[6], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
    h_2995_str = fmt_time(table_hours[7], unit=ureg.hour, precision=1)
```

### Sample size requirements per empirical claim {#sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim}

The reliability claim, rather than the facility schedule, dictates the necessary sample size. For a zero-failure campaign the count is @eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size, with the rule of three as its rare-failure approximation; @fig-07-confidence-bounds plots it across confidence levels and @tbl-07-confidence-bounds tabulates it. The order of operations is what this subsection adds. The claim (target and confidence) is fixed first, the count follows from it, and if a testing facility cannot afford that count, the engineering team must narrow its claim rather than present an underpowered test as formal qualification. If a campaign records any failure, it must apply the general binomial bound of @sec-evaluation-bounds-with-failures; an engineering team cannot salvage a zero-failure claim by appending clean runs after inspecting intermediate data.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The same bound, counted in operating hours rather than trials, and the population such a statistic describes are developed in @sec-verification-exposure-wall.
:::

### Physical experimentation costs and hardware fatigue budgeting {#sec-evaluation-trial-costs}

The door-opening campaign illustrates how the physical cost of a single trial accumulates. During a nominal execution run, the mobile base navigates inward from its `{python} EvalMachine.standoff_str` standoff position and stops. The manipulator arm then executes a guarded unlatching sequence at `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` and swings the door open. These physical motions occupy `{python} DoorCycle.t_run_str` of active test-cell time. Preparing the testbed for the next statistically independent draw requires an automated reset: re-latching the door mechanism, navigating the base back to its standoff position, and flushing onboard telemetry buffers. This reset sequence adds `{python} DoorCycle.t_reset_str`, bringing the total wall-clock budget for each trial to `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str`. At this cycle duration, the initial twenty clean runs take `{python} DoorCycle.t_opening_str`. Qualifying a 99.9 percent success lower limit (notebook \ref{nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance}) demands a dramatically larger campaign, even before accounting for the thermal cooldown intervals required by the actuator windings.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The recovery time a periodic duty cycle forces between loaded bursts, before the windings reach their temperature ceiling, is established in @sec-body-transient-thermal-bursts.
:::

::: {#nbk-evaluation-statistical-scaling-high-reliability-assurance .callout-notebook title="The nines tax"}

**Problem**: An evaluation target calls for a one-sided success lower limit of $\TargetTrialSuccessProbability = 0.999$ at 95 percent confidence. How many zero-failure door runs does it need, and how long does the latch cell take to supply them?

**Variables**:

* $\TargetTrialSuccessProbability = 0.999$ and $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str` (Chosen; the claim).
* $\TrialRunTime =$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_run_str` and $\TrialResetLatency =$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_reset_str` (Illustrative; drive-in, guarded unlatch, swing, then re-latch and return), so $\VerificationTrialTime =$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str`.
* `{python} DoorCycle.n_operators_str` safety operators per run (Illustrative).

**Math**: From @eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size, $\ZeroFailureTrialCount = \lceil \ln(1/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel) / \ln(1/\TargetTrialSuccessProbability) \rceil = \lceil$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.ln_inv_alpha_str` $/$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.ln_inv_999_str` $\rceil =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str`, close to the rule of three's $3/(1-\TargetTrialSuccessProbability)$. The cell time is `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` $\times$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` $=$ `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_s_str`, or `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_str` (`{python} DoorCycle.t_target_days_str`) of continuous testing, and `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_operator_str` of operator time, over `{python} DoorCycle.shifts_floor_str` eight-hour shifts.

**Result**: `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` clean runs and `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_str` of cell occupancy, against `{python} DoorCycle.t_opening_str` for the opening twenty.

**Systems insight**: The denominator $\ln(1/\TargetTrialSuccessProbability) \approx 1 - \TargetTrialSuccessProbability$ shrinks tenfold with each added nine, so each nine multiplies the runs, the cell hours, and the wear by ten; a longer cycle scales the hours in proportion. A campaign this long also outlives the stationarity it assumes, and a component replaced midway may require a new population definition rather than pooling incompatible runs.

:::

     "29", "299", "2,995 trials" = runs_for(0.9/0.99/0.999, 0.95) in the figure cell, which checks 2,995 against

(b) The same limits read as failure upper limits on log axes fall one decade per decade of runs, so each further nine costs ten times the trials: 99.9 percent needs `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` runs, or `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_str` at the `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` door cycle." fig-alt="Two panels sharing a log-scale axis of zero-failure trial count from 10 to about 4,000, each with dotted, solid, and dashed curves for 90, 95, and 99 percent confidence. Panel (a) plots the success lower confidence limit in percent: the curves rise steeply, the 95 percent curve is marked at 86.1 percent success lower and 13.9 percent failure upper for 20 trials, and all three curves bunch together below a dashed 99.9 percent target line. Panel (b) plots the failure upper confidence limit on a log axis as three parallel falling straight lines, with the 95 percent line marked at 10 percent for 29 trials, 1 percent for 299 trials, and 0.1 percent for 2,995 trials, the last annotated as 33.3 hours at 40 seconds per run."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOPPER-PEARSON SUCCESS LOWER LIMITS AFTER ZERO FAILURES (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-07-confidence-bounds
# │ Goal:    show what a clean run of n physical trials can and cannot certify
# │ Show:    (a) the lower limit against trial count, at three confidence
# │          levels; (b) the failure upper limit on log axes, where each
# │          further nine costs ten times the trials
# │ How:     p_lower = (1 - c)**(1/n); every annotated value is derived here
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

_fig, _ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.2))
plt.close(_fig)
fig, (ax, ax_f) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.2))

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario parameters) ────────────────────────────────────────────
CONFIDENCES = (0.90, 0.95, 0.99)  # category: chosen; plotted confidence levels
TARGET = 0.999  # category: chosen; the success lower limit the chapter argues toward
CYCLE_SECONDS = DoorCycle.t_cycle.to(ureg.second).magnitude  # category: illustrative; door cycle from calc-evaluation-door-cycle
REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE = 0.95  # category: chosen; the level both annotations read off
NINES = (0.9, 0.99, 0.999)  # category: chosen; success lower limits marked on panel (b)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def lower_limit(n, confidence):
    """One-sided Clopper-Pearson lower limit on success given zero failures."""
    return 100.0 * (1.0 - confidence) ** (1.0 / n)

def runs_for(target, confidence):
    """Zero-failure runs needed for a success lower limit of target."""
    return int(np.ceil(np.log(1.0 - confidence) / np.log(target)))

n = np.logspace(1, np.log10(4200), 600)
small_n = 20
big_n = runs_for(TARGET, REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE)
nine_runs = [runs_for(t, REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE) for t in NINES]
check(big_n == ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999, "figure and LEGO cell must agree on the 99.9 percent run count")
check(all(9 < b / a < 11 for a, b in zip(nine_runs, nine_runs[1:])), "each further nine must cost about ten times the runs")

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Ordered categories, not resources: one hue, distinguished by dash pattern.
DASHES = [(0, (1, 2)), (0, ()), (0, (6, 3))]
for confidence, dash in zip(CONFIDENCES, DASHES):
    ax.plot(n, lower_limit(n, confidence), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.0, linestyle=dash, label=f"{confidence:.0%} confidence")
    ax_f.plot(n, 100.0 - lower_limit(n, confidence), color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=2.0, linestyle=dash)

# (a) Success lower limit on a linear axis: the fast early gain.
ax.axhline(100.0 * TARGET, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=1.0, linestyle=(0, (5, 4)))
ax.text(10.6, 99.1, f"{100 * TARGET:.1f}% statistical target", fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["primary"], va="top")
box = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc="white", ec=COLORS["grid"], lw=1.0)
arrow = dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=4)
y_small = lower_limit(small_n, REFERENCE_CONFIDENCE)
ax.plot([small_n], [y_small], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"{small_n:,} trials\n{y_small:.1f}% success lower\n{100 - y_small:.1f}% failure upper",
    xy=(small_n, y_small),
    xytext=(48, 74),
    textcoords="data",
    fontsize=8.5,
    bbox=box,
    arrowprops=arrow,
    va="center",
    ha="left",
)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(10, 4200)
ax.set_ylim(60, 100.4)
ax.set_yticks(range(60, 101, 5))
ax.set_xlabel("Zero-failure trial count n (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Success lower confidence limit (%)")
ax.set_title("(a) Success lower limit", loc="left", fontsize=10)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8.5)

# (b) Failure upper limit on log axes: each nine is one decade of trials.
for target, n_pt in zip(NINES, nine_runs):
    f_pt = 100.0 * (1.0 - target)
    ax_f.plot([10, n_pt], [f_pt, f_pt], color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.9, zorder=1)
    ax_f.plot([n_pt, n_pt], [0.03, f_pt], color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.9, zorder=1)
    ax_f.plot([n_pt], [f_pt], "o", ms=6, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], zorder=5)
    label = f"{n_pt:,} trials"
    if n_pt == big_n:
        label += f"\n{n_pt * CYCLE_SECONDS / 3600:.1f} h at {CYCLE_SECONDS:.0f} s/run"
    ax_f.text(n_pt * 0.9, f_pt * 0.55, label, fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["primary"], ha="right", va="top")
ax_f.set_xscale("log")
ax_f.set_yscale("log")
ax_f.set_xlim(10, 4200)
ax_f.set_ylim(0.03, 40)
ax_f.set_yticks([0.1, 1, 10])
ax_f.set_yticklabels(["0.1", "1", "10"])
ax_f.set_xlabel("Zero-failure trial count n (log scale)")
ax_f.set_ylabel("Failure upper confidence limit (%, log scale)")
ax_f.set_title("(b) Failure upper limit, 95% confidence marked", loc="left", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The two panels of @fig-07-confidence-bounds separate two lessons. Early clean runs buy confidence cheaply, and the 95 percent lower limit already reaches `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` after twenty runs. Past that point the curves crowd under the 99.9 percent target, and the confidence level matters far less than the target itself. On log axes the failure upper limit falls only one decade per decade of trials, so the last nine is the expensive one: `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` runs, or `{python} DoorCycle.t_target_str` of test-cell time at the door cycle.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-confidence-table
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ZERO-FAILURE CONFIDENCE LIMITS FOR THE BOUNDS TABLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-07-confidence-bounds (statistics columns).
# │ Show: one-sided success lower limits at 90, 95, and 99 percent confidence
# │       and the 95 percent failure upper limit for each table row.
# │ How: p_lower = (1 - C)^(1/n) via calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound;
# │      rows are DoorCycle.table_n so the time column and these stay aligned.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, check

class ConfidenceBoundsTable:
    """Clopper-Pearson zero-failure limits for every row of the bounds table."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    table_n = DoorCycle.table_n  # category: chosen; rows of @tbl-07-confidence-bounds

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    lo90 = [calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n, confidence=0.90) for n in table_n]
    lo95 = [calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n, confidence=0.95) for n in table_n]
    lo99 = [calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n, confidence=0.99) for n in table_n]
    up95 = [1.0 - p for p in lo95]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(lo95[1] - ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower) < 1e-12, "20-run row must match the opening campaign's bound")
    check(abs(lo95[-1] - 0.999) < 1e-4, "Last row must meet the 99.9 percent target")
    check(all(a < b < c for a, b, c in zip(lo99, lo95, lo90)), "Higher confidence must give a lower success limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    lo90_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in lo90]
    lo95_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in lo95]
    lo99_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in lo99]
    up95_str = [fmt_percent(p, precision=2, style="symbol") for p in up95]
```

| Zero-failure trials $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ |                      90% lower success limit |                      95% lower success limit |                      99% lower success limit |                      95% upper failure limit |         Test time at door cycle | Interpretation under iid test draws                |
|:---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------|
| 10                                           | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[0]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[0]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[0]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[0]` |   `{python} DoorCycle.h_10_str` | Wide uncertainty; no observed failures             |
| 20                                           | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[1]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[1]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[1]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[1]` |   `{python} DoorCycle.h_20_str` | Bound applies only to the sampled distribution     |
| 50                                           | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[2]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[2]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[2]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[2]` |   `{python} DoorCycle.h_50_str` | More evidence; untested conditions remain          |
| 100                                          | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[3]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[3]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[3]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[3]` |  `{python} DoorCycle.h_100_str` | No deployment permission follows from the interval |
| 250                                          | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[4]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[4]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[4]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[4]` |  `{python} DoorCycle.h_250_str` | Check hardware and sampling stationarity           |
| 500                                          | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[5]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[5]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[5]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[5]` |  `{python} DoorCycle.h_500_str` | Bound remains tied to declared conditions          |
| 1,000                                        | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[6]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[6]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[6]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[6]` | `{python} DoorCycle.h_1000_str` | Below a 99.9% lower-limit target                   |
| 2,995                                        | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo90_str[7]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo95_str[7]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.lo99_str[7]` | `{python} ConfidenceBoundsTable.up95_str[7]` | `{python} DoorCycle.h_2995_str` | Meets that statistical target if assumptions hold  |

: **One-sided binomial confidence limits after zero failures**: Success lower limits are $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel^{1/\ZeroFailureTrialCount}$ and the corresponding failure upper limit is $1-0.05^{1/\ZeroFailureTrialCount}$. Test times use the `{python} DoorCycle.t_cycle_str` door cycle. {#tbl-07-confidence-bounds tbl-colwidths="[11,12,12,12,13,12,28]"}

The physical plant also degrades as trials accumulate. Statistical confidence bounds assume iid draws from a stationary process, but physical wear breaks stationarity. Transmission backlash (lost motion), effective wheel radius, tire surface friction, and joint damping all drift at rates that engineers must monitor directly on the test hardware. Naively pooling a thousand trials implicitly treats an evolving, degrading machine as an unchanging platform. A failure on trial 950 may reflect testbed wear, a policy limitation, or their interaction; configuration and condition logs are needed to distinguish these causes.

Trials this expensive make stopping early attractive. A fixed-sample, zero-failure protocol already permits safe early rejection: testing halts immediately upon the first observed failure, avoiding pointless exposure to a hazardous policy. Early acceptance, however, presents a different statistical challenge. Halting testing prematurely simply because intermediate results appear favorable inflates the false-positive rate unless the stopping threshold was calibrated in advance. To balance test efficiency with rigorous error guarantees, @sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt develops sequential boundaries for both acceptance and rejection.

### Sequential probability ratio testing {#sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt}

Permitting early acceptance requires a decision boundary calibrated before executing the first trial. Wald's sequential probability ratio test (SPRT)[^fn-wald-sprt-origin] [@wald1945sequential] provides this mechanism by evaluating the cumulative log-likelihood ratio after each successive trial, comparing an unacceptable failure rate against an acceptable one. For a strict autonomy campaign, the Bernoulli outcome records unassisted task completion; for a full-system service evaluation, it records the separately specified operational outcome. While the mathematical formulation accommodates either metric, the outcome definition must remain strictly frozen throughout data collection.
