
:::

Empirical road testing demonstrates concretely what fleet-scale operational exposure can and cannot substantiate. The first benchmark evaluated in the RAND study represents the exposure wall translated into driving mileage: given an average human driver fatality rate of `{python} AvExposure.rate_fatal_str` per 100 million miles, an autonomous vehicle fleet must log `{python} AvExposure.miles_fatal_zero_str` million failure-free miles simply to establish an upper bound matching the human baseline at 95 percent confidence. That single demonstration requires approximately `{python} AvExposure.fatal_zero_ratio_str` times the total rider-only commercial mileage accumulated by Waymo through January 2025 (`{python} AvExposure.waymo_ro_miles_str` million miles). Producing an empirical estimate of the fatality rate within a 20 percent margin of error requires `{python} AvExposure.miles_fatal_prec_str` billion miles.

Nevertheless, tens of millions of operational miles can validate claims regarding higher-frequency events. @kusano2025comparison evaluated crashed-vehicle rates across `{python} AvExposure.waymo_ro_miles_str` million rider-only miles against human driving benchmarks matched for vehicle class, road type, and operating jurisdiction. They demonstrated a `{python} AvExposure.waymo_injury_reduction_str` percent reduction in police-reported injury crashes and an `{python} AvExposure.waymo_airbag_reduction_str` percent reduction in airbag-deployment collisions, both with confidence intervals strictly bounded away from zero. The underlying statistical principle is direct: a finite operational exposure bounds only those event classes whose expected occurrence counts within that window are statistically meaningful. Any rigorous comparative safety claim requires an exposure-matched baseline and confidence intervals over the incident rate ratio. The rarest, most catastrophic failure modes remain fundamentally untestable through on-road fleet mileage alone, and simulated driving mileage adds no true physical exposure to these empirical totals.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-mtbf-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MTBF EXPOSURE CAMPAIGN ON THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the MTBF worked example after @fig-07-av-miles-scaling and
# │          @chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf.
# │ Show: exposure hours, zero-failure missions, calendar time, and wheel
# │       revolutions a single machine needs to bound a 1e-4 per hour rate.
# │       The hub bearings' L10 rating is not in the data sheet (needs source),
# │       so the prose names the measurement instead of comparing against it.
# │ How: T = -ln(alpha) / lambda via calc_empirical_testing_exposure;
# │      N = ln(alpha) / ln(1 - lambda t_mission); N_rev = N v t / (pi D).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_time, fmt_math, sci_latex, fmt, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MtbfCampaign:
    """Zero-failure mission campaign that bounds a 1e-4 per hour rate on one machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen; one-sided confidence level
    rate = 1e-4 / ureg.hour  # category: chosen; teaching target (MTBF 10,000 h)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit
    t_mission = 360.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; one retrieval mission
    t_reset = 120.0 * ureg.second  # category: illustrative; dock recharge and telemetry reset
    d_wheel = RM.drive_unit.wheel_diameter  # category: datasheet; direct-drive hub-motor wheel (ZLTECH ZLLG10ASM800-48)
    mtbf_relaxed = 1000.0 * ureg.hour  # category: chosen; relaxed target in @chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 1 - confidence
    t_cycle = t_mission + t_reset
    d_mission = (v * t_mission).to(ureg.meter)
    t_continuous = calc_empirical_testing_exposure(rate, confidence=confidence).to(ureg.hour)
    p_fail_mission = (rate * t_mission).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    n_req = math.log(alpha) / math.log(1 - p_fail_mission)
    t_calendar = (n_req * t_cycle).to(ureg.hour)
    n_rev = (n_req * d_mission / (math.pi * d_wheel)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Drive limit is not 1.5 m/s")
    check(abs(t_continuous.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 29957) < 1, "Continuous exposure should be about 29,957 h")
    check(abs(n_req - 299572) < 2, "Zero-failure missions should be about 299,572")
    check(abs(t_calendar.to(ureg.hour).magnitude - 39943) < 1, "Calendar time should be about 39,943 h")
    check(abs(d_mission.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 540) < 1e-6, "Mission distance should be 540 m")
    check(abs(d_wheel.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 266.0) < 1e-9, "Hub-motor wheel diameter is not 266 mm")
    check(abs(n_rev - 1.94e8) < 0.01e8, "Wheel revolutions should be about 1.94e8")
    check(
        calc_empirical_testing_exposure(1 / mtbf_relaxed, confidence=confidence) < 1.0 * ureg.year,
        "The relaxed target must fit in one rig-year (checkpoint)",
    )
    # margin_exposure_wall_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 33.3, 29,957, 3.0 million, and 3.0 billion hours
    check(
        f"{DoorCycle.t_target.to(ureg.hour).magnitude:.1f}" == "33.3"
        and round(t_continuous.to(ureg.hour).magnitude) == 29957
        and f"{ExposureWall.t_e6.to(ureg.hour).magnitude / 1e6:.1f}" == "3.0"
        and f"{ExposureWall.t_e9.to(ureg.hour).magnitude / 1e9:.1f}" == "3.0",
        "Exposure-wall ladder fig-alt values changed",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
    d_mission_str = fmt_length(d_mission, precision=0)
    t_mission_str = fmt_time(t_mission, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_reset_str = fmt_time(t_reset, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    t_cycle_str = fmt_time(t_cycle, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    d_wheel_str = fmt_length(d_wheel, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    t_continuous_str = fmt_int(round(t_continuous.to(ureg.hour).magnitude), commas=True)
    yr_continuous_str = fmt(t_continuous.to(ureg.year).magnitude, precision=2)
    n_req_str = fmt_int(round(n_req), commas=True)
    t_calendar_str = fmt_int(round(t_calendar.to(ureg.hour).magnitude), commas=True)
    yr_calendar_str = fmt(t_calendar.to(ureg.year).magnitude, precision=2)
    n_rev_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(n_rev, precision=2))
    t_mission_h_str = fmt_time(t_mission, unit=ureg.hour, precision=2)
    p_fail_mission_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(p_fail_mission, precision=1))
    mtbf_relaxed_str = fmt_time(mtbf_relaxed, unit=ureg.hour, precision=0, commas=True)
```

The exposure wall restricts verification even for target failure rates orders of magnitude less stringent than aerospace standards. Consider an industrial requirement for the warehouse mobile manipulator: the platform must certify a critical failure rate $\ConstantHazardRate \le 1.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ failures/hour}$, corresponding to a Mean Time Between Critical Failures of $\text{MTBF} \ge 10{,}000\text{ hours}$[^fn-mtbf-constant-rate] at a 95 percent statistical confidence level ($\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel = 0.05$). In this operational scenario, each warehouse retrieval mission takes $\MissionDuration =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_mission_str` (`{python} MtbfCampaign.t_mission_h_str`) and covers `{python} MtbfCampaign.d_mission_str` at the platform's `{python} MtbfCampaign.v_str` maximum drive velocity. Automated docking, battery replenishment, and telemetry offloading introduce an overhead of $\ResetLatency =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_reset_str`, resulting in a total cycle duration of `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_cycle_str` per trial. Each drive wheel uses a direct-drive hub motor with an outer diameter $\WheelDiameter =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.d_wheel_str`, eliminating mechanical gearbox reduction between the motor and the wheel rim.

[^fn-mtbf-constant-rate]: **MTBF and a Constant Rate**\index{MTBF!constant failure rate}: The constant-rate model used here describes the flat middle of the bathtub curve after burn-in; it makes the reciprocal rate an MTBF and supports the zero-event bound $\FailureObservationInterval \ge 3/\ConstantHazardRate$. Wear-out mechanisms such as bearing fatigue raise the rate as revolutions accumulate, so a rate bounded this way says nothing about wear-out life, which the $\RatedFatigueLife$ rating below addresses separately.

Applying @eq-eval-exposure-wall reveals that establishing this $10^{-4}\text{ failures/hour}$ ceiling without observing a single failure requires `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_continuous_str` hours (`{python} MtbfCampaign.yr_continuous_str` years) of continuous, uninterrupted operation. Discretized across operational sorties, each mission has an allocated failure probability budget of $\TrialFailureProbability \le \ConstantHazardRate \cdot \MissionDuration =$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.p_fail_mission_math`. Inverting the zero-failure binomial model from @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival yields $\ZeroFailureTrialCount = \ln(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel)/\ln(1-\TrialFailureProbability)$, demanding `{python} MtbfCampaign.n_req_str` consecutive clean missions. This total dwarfs typical empirical validation budgets, which rarely exceed hundreds or thousands of runs. Conducting these trials sequentially on a single physical machine at `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_cycle_str` per cycle requires `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_calendar_str` elapsed hours (`{python} MtbfCampaign.yr_calendar_str` calendar years) and subjects each direct-drive wheel to $\WheelRevolutionCount = (\ZeroFailureTrialCount \cdot \BaseForwardSpeed \cdot \MissionDuration) / (\pi \WheelDiameter) \approx$ `{python} MtbfCampaign.n_rev_math` continuous revolutions.

Because the hub motor drives the wheel without an intermediate gearbox, every wheel revolution directly rotates the internal hub bearings. Mechanical component reliability is governed by the bearing rated life, $\RatedFatigueLife$\index{Bearing life!L10}, the number of operating revolutions that 90 percent of an identical bearing cohort completes before initiating fatigue flaking under a specified radial and axial load. $\RatedFatigueLife$ is an empirical population metric rather than an abrupt wear-out threshold, and it degrades steeply as the carried load increases. Determining whether this test campaign exhausts the mechanical endurance of the running gear requires comparing $\WheelRevolutionCount$ against the manufacturer's internal bearing load rating and measuring the actual static and dynamic wheel reactions with corner-scale load cells. This is the stationarity problem of @sec-evaluation-trial-costs at the scale of a reliability campaign. The revolution count states how much wear the campaign itself inflicts, and only an $\RatedFatigueLife$ rating at the measured load can say whether that wear reaches the fatigue regime. Because hub-motor datasheets rarely disclose that internal load rating, a campaign of this duration cannot be shown to stay clear of wear-out until the load is measured. Systems teams must therefore schedule, log, and isolate component refurbishments and sensor recalibrations before pooling runs across extended operating intervals.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-intervention-campaign
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INTERVENTION RATE OF A SUPERVISED MISSION CAMPAIGN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the censored-trial example after the MTBF campaign.
# │ Show: active hours, distance, MTBI, intervention density, and an exact
# │       95 percent interval on the intervention rate for 38 interventions in
# │       100 retrieval missions of the MTBF campaign's mission.
# │ How: T = n t_mission; L = n d_mission; MTBI = T / N; D = N / L; the Garwood
# │      interval solves the Poisson tails P(N >= k) = P(N <= k) = alpha / 2.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_time, fmt_length, check

def _poisson_cdf(k, mu):
    """P(N <= k) for N ~ Poisson(mu)."""
    term, total = math.exp(-mu), math.exp(-mu)
    for j in range(1, k + 1):
        term *= mu / j
        total += term
    return total

def _garwood(k, alpha):
    """Exact two-sided (1 - alpha) interval on a Poisson mean after k events."""

    def _solve(f):
        lo, hi = 0.0, 10.0 * (k + 10)
        for _ in range(200):
            mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
            lo, hi = (mid, hi) if f(mid) > 0 else (lo, mid)
        return 0.5 * (lo + hi)

    lower = 0.0 if k == 0 else _solve(lambda mu: alpha / 2 - (1.0 - _poisson_cdf(k - 1, mu)))
    upper = _solve(lambda mu: _poisson_cdf(k, mu) - alpha / 2)
    return lower, upper

class InterventionCampaign:
    """Supervised mission campaign: intervention burden, not failure rate."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_missions = 100  # category: illustrative; retrieval missions in the supervised campaign
    n_int = 38  # category: illustrative; recorded interventions of the declared class
    t_mission = MtbfCampaign.t_mission  # category: illustrative; one retrieval mission (MTBF campaign)
    d_mission = MtbfCampaign.d_mission  # category: derived; mission distance at the drive limit
    alpha = 0.05  # category: chosen; two-sided interval level

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_active = (n_missions * t_mission).to(hour)
    d_total = (n_missions * d_mission).to(kilometer)
    mtbi = (t_active / n_int).to(minute)
    d_int = (n_int / d_total).to(1 / kilometer)
    rate = (n_int / t_active).to(1 / hour)
    _lo, _hi = _garwood(n_int, alpha)
    rate_lo = (_lo / t_active).to(1 / hour)
    rate_hi = (_hi / t_active).to(1 / hour)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_active.to(hour).magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "100 missions of 360 s must be 10 active hours")
    check(abs(d_total.to(kilometer).magnitude - 54.0) < 1e-9, "100 missions of 540 m must be 54 km")
    check(abs(mtbi.to(minute).magnitude - 15.79) < 0.01, "MTBI should be about 15.8 min")
    check(abs(d_int.magnitude - 0.704) < 0.001, "Intervention density should be about 0.70 per km")
    check(abs(_lo - 26.89) < 0.01 and abs(_hi - 52.16) < 0.01, "Garwood interval for 38 events should be 26.9 to 52.2")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_missions_str = fmt_int(n_missions)
    n_int_str = fmt_int(n_int)
    t_active_str = fmt_time(t_active, unit=hour, precision=0)
    d_total_str = fmt_length(d_total, unit=kilometer, precision=0)
    mtbi_str = fmt_time(mtbi, unit=minute, precision=1)
    d_int_str = fmt(d_int.magnitude, precision=2)
    rate_str = fmt(rate.magnitude, precision=1)
    rate_lo_str = fmt(rate_lo.magnitude, precision=1)
    rate_hi_str = fmt(rate_hi.magnitude, precision=1)
```

The distinction drawn in @sec-evaluation-what-measured between MTBF and the intervention-based metrics matters most in a supervised campaign. When operating with real-time safety guardrails, permission-path filters, software limits, emergency stops, and human supervisor overrides can intercept hazardous trajectories before physical damage occurs when their sensing, response, and physical margins are qualified for those conditions. Such interventions censor the unassisted physical outcome while remaining recorded autonomy failures. The campaign measures an empirical intervention rate, $\InterventionRate = \TotalInterventionCount/\CampaignActiveTime$, whose inverse is the MTBI.

Consider an evaluation run in which the permission path or human supervisors intervene `{python} InterventionCampaign.n_int_str` times during `{python} InterventionCampaign.n_missions_str` retrieval missions configured identically to the scenario above. With each sortie lasting `{python} MtbfCampaign.t_mission_str` and covering `{python} MtbfCampaign.d_mission_str`, the campaign aggregates `{python} InterventionCampaign.t_active_str` of active physical movement across `{python} InterventionCampaign.d_total_str`. These trials yield an MTBI of approximately `{python} InterventionCampaign.mtbi_str` and an intervention spatial density of `{python} InterventionCampaign.d_int_str` per kilometer. Because interventions occur frequently throughout the campaign, the resulting rate parameter supports rigorous statistical inference: modeling interventions as a Poisson arrival process, the exact 95 percent Garwood confidence interval for $\InterventionRate$ spans `{python} InterventionCampaign.rate_lo_str` to `{python} InterventionCampaign.rate_hi_str` interventions per active operating hour around the empirical mean of `{python} InterventionCampaign.rate_str` [@garwood1936fiducial].

A system can achieve zero hardware damage while simultaneously imposing an intolerable intervention overhead. Aggregate intervention counts do not reveal ACR, because multiple interventions can cluster within a single difficult run, while other missions might abort without triggering a formal intervention. Determining autonomous completion requires inspecting the cycle-by-cycle mission ledger. Furthermore, observing zero hardware damage across `{python} InterventionCampaign.t_active_str` of supervised testing provides zero statistical evidence that the unassisted policy possesses an MTBF of `{python} InterventionCampaign.t_active_str`. From the standpoint of unassisted physical reliability, every intervened mission represents a right-censored observation: the safety layer terminated the trial before its unconstrained physical trajectory could unfold. The log captures neither a confirmed physical disaster nor an autonomous success. Interpreting these censored runs as demonstrations of unassisted task survival commits the censored trial fallacy detailed in @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes. In deployment budgets, the reset and recalibration latency following each intervention represents an unavoidable operational penalty.

### Peak loads and unvisited conditions

Operating exposure represents only one dimension of the verification ceiling. A deeper epistemic boundary stems from the fact that safety-constrained testing systematically censors the very physical regimes that pose the greatest operational risk (@sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes). Because a destructive physical failure cannot be undone (the first law, irreversibility), supervisory safety interlocks must truncate trajectories before structural damage occurs. The empirical record terminates exactly where the intervention fires.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The first law, irreversibility, which holds that work delivered to the plant cannot be rolled back, is established in @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws.
:::

This constraint creates an unavoidable paradox in embodied evaluation. The corner cases an engineering team most urgently needs to characterize, such as loss of traction on slick surfaces at maximum transit speed, dynamic wheel slip, or imminent collisions in tight aisles, are precisely the physical regimes the system cannot be permitted to explore. Allowing an automated mobile manipulator to skid into structural shelving damages the drive chassis, knocks calibrated lidar and camera constellations out of alignment, and sidelines the entire test cell for mechanical repair. Physical cages, virtual geofences, and human operators with emergency stops truncate trials at a conservative safety boundary. The test log records an intervention event, but the downstream physical consequences of the policy's unconstrained commands remain unobserved. The intervention is tallied in the denominator of the operational exposure log, while the true open-loop consequence of the control proposal remains unmeasured.

```{python}
#| label: calc-evaluation-mean-vs-peak
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEAN CONTACT FORCE VERSUS PEAK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Peak loads and unvisited conditions" in @sec-evaluation-limits.
# │ Show: an illustrative policy whose mean latch force sits under the contact
# │       tripwire while its 99th-percentile peak exceeds the latch limit.
# │ How: stipulated values; guards pin the ordering the prose relies on.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_force, check

class MeanVsPeak:
    """A benign mean and a damaging tail on the latch."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_mean = 12.0 * ureg.newton  # category: illustrative; mean latch contact force over nominal trials
    f_p99 = 115.0 * ureg.newton  # category: illustrative; 99th-percentile peak at an angular offset

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(f_mean < EvalMachine.f_trip, "The mean must sit below the contact tripwire")
    check(f_p99 > EvalMachine.f_latch_limit, "The tail must exceed the latch limit")
    # margin_latch_peak_force_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 12, 115, 100, and 15 newtons
    check(
        [round(f.to(newton).magnitude) for f in (f_mean, f_p99, EvalMachine.f_latch_limit, EvalMachine.f_trip)] == [12, 115, 100, 15],
        "Latch peak envelope fig-alt values changed",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_mean_str = fmt_force(f_mean, precision=0)
    f_p99_str = fmt_force(f_p99, precision=0)
```

When evaluating physical hardware survival, average metrics can mask catastrophic structural overloads. Consider a learned mobile manipulation policy whose average latch contact force across one hundred nominal trials is only $\MeanLatchContactForce =$ `{python} MeanVsPeak.f_mean_str`, below the `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` contact tripwire threshold. However, if the gripper strikes the strike plate at a slight angular offset, the tail of the empirical peak-force distribution exhibits a 99th-percentile impact of `{python} MeanVsPeak.f_p99_str`. This transient peak breaches the structural latch limit of `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str` despite the benign average. A peak of that size in a campaign guarded by a `{python} EvalMachine.f_trip_str` tripwire is not a contradiction. The first impact peak arrives faster than the tripwire can act, so these trials record the overshoot first and are ended by the tripwire afterward, as failures; the rise-time argument below shows why no reactive monitor can prevent it. While a single force peak does not directly equate to total impulse or plastic deformation (which depend on the full force-time profile, structural load paths, and material yield criteria), it reveals how central tendencies conceal destructive tail behavior.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_latch_peak_force_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars of latch contact force against a red dashed latch limit of 100 newtons. The mean of 12 newtons sits left of a dotted tripwire at 15 newtons, and the 99th-percentile peak of 115 newtons runs past the limit into the shaded region."}
*A `{python} MeanVsPeak.f_mean_str` mean hides a `{python} MeanVsPeak.f_p99_str` peak past the `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str` limit.*
:::

The undamped spring-mass model of @eq-training-impact-peak, which in @sec-training-contact-exploit exposed how a soft simulated spring understated the latch force, bounds this initial impact\index{Contact impact!approach-speed bound}. Written for evaluation, its moving mass becomes the reduced mass of the colliding bodies, $\ReducedImpactMass = (1/\EffectiveImpactMass + 1/\StruckObjectMass)^{-1}$, which reduces to the arm's effective inertia against an immovable frame, and its spring becomes the local contact stiffness $\ContactStiffness$. The peak force is then $\ContactApproachSpeed\sqrt{\ReducedImpactMass\,\ContactStiffness}$, and it arrives a quarter of the natural oscillation period after touch, a rise time of $\FiniteChange \ImpactRiseTime \approx (\pi/2)\sqrt{\ReducedImpactMass/\ContactStiffness}$. Inverting the peak for a structural threshold $\LatchForceLimit$ gives the quantity an evaluation campaign can actually enforce, a precontact speed limit:
$$\ContactApproachSpeed \le \frac{\LatchForceLimit}{\sqrt{\ReducedImpactMass\, \ContactStiffness}},$$ {#eq-eval-impact-speed}
This physical relationship governs the transient contact velocity limits in ISO/TS 15066 Annex A for power- and force-limited collaborative robots [@isots15066]. The collaborative application requirements of ISO/TS 15066 have since been incorporated into ISO 10218-2:2025, and ISO/TS 15066:2016 remains published while it is revised into the international standard ISO 15066-1 [@iso10218part2].

Evaluating this bound on a physical door latch requires measuring both the effective mass of the arm at the end-effector and the local contact stiffness of the latch mechanism, parameters that depend heavily on joint posture and kinematics, and are never found in high-level hardware datasheets. The systems takeaway, however, is structural rather than numerical. If a software monitor's sensing, compute, and actuation latency exceeds the mechanical rise time $\FiniteChange \ImpactRiseTime$, no reactive software policy can attenuate the initial force spike, regardless of model inference speed. Software intervention comes too late. Physical protection against initial impact must therefore rely on two pre-contact mechanisms: passive mechanical compliance, which lowers effective stiffness $\ContactStiffness$ and extends rise time $\FiniteChange \ImpactRiseTime$, and strict pre-contact kinematic velocity caps, such as the platform's `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach limit.

Extreme value theory (EVT)\index{Extreme value theory} provides asymptotic statistical distributions for modeling such tail extremes. However, fitting a generalized extreme value family (Gumbel, Fréchet, or Weibull) requires a substantial corpus of independent block maxima, verified through goodness-of-fit testing and reported with rigorous confidence bounds. The physical mechanics of contact do not prescribe which parametric tail family applies.[^fn-math-extreme-value] In the absence of thousands of destructive physical trials, @tbl-07-extreme-value-tails pairs measurable physical disturbance channels with concrete architectural safeguards rather than relying on unverified tail extrapolations.

[^fn-math-extreme-value]: **Extreme Value Theory**\index{Extreme value theory!origins}: @fisher1928limiting found the three limiting forms that the largest member of a large sample can take, @gnedenko1943distribution proved that under general conditions no other limits exist, and @gumbel1958statistics made the theory an engineering tool for floods and material fatigue. Each of those applications fitted many block maxima. The latch campaign yields one maximum per run, twenty in all, too few to choose a family, let alone fit one.

| Disturbance channel     | Peak quantity and sampling record                    | Physical consequence to test                             | Candidate protection to validate                                                  |
|:------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Compute and bus latency | Per-cycle end-to-end age and deadline misses         | Stale proposals erode braking margin                     | Chunk lease and independently timed fallback                                      |
| Contact shock           | Force-time trace, impulse, and peak at the load path | Yield or overload before a reactive command takes effect | Passive compliance and precontact speed limit; reactive limits address later load |
| Low traction            | Local friction estimate and stopping response        | Slip extends stopping distance                           | Conservative speed ceiling and tested fallback on low-grip surfaces               |
| Optical glare           | Saturation duration and perception misses            | False clearance or lost state estimate                   | Redundant sensing and independent physical constraints                            |

: **Peak-disturbance evidence and protection**: Mechanisms identify measurements and safeguards, not an EVT family or event rate. Any quantitative tail claim needs a defined population, fitted model, goodness-of-fit checks, and uncertainty. {#tbl-07-extreme-value-tails tbl-colwidths="[18,28,26,28]"}

The door latch campaign shows why the contact shock entry in @tbl-07-extreme-value-tails pairs a measurement with an architectural safeguard rather than with a fitted tail. Each trial yields only one block maximum, its peak latch contact force, and twenty maxima cannot fit a generalized extreme value tail that would predict the probability of exceeding `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str`. The safeguard therefore comes from the rise-time argument above. The guarded `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` approach is a candidate precontact limit whose adequacy depends on the measured effective mass, contact stiffness, and structural threshold; reactive force monitoring addresses the sustained load that follows.

Deploying parallel robots across a test fleet does not establish statistical independence. Ten identical machines operating concurrently in a single warehouse share the same manufacturing batch, firmware revision, concrete sealant finish, heating and ventilation airflow, and operator handling protocols. Environmental disturbances absent from that facility, such as low-angle winter solar glare, surface water pooling, or floor polishing glazing, affect none of the machines. Ten thousand fleet hours accumulated within a single facility are ten thousand hours of exposure to one site's conditions, not ten thousand hours of operational diversity. Standardized physical test fixtures, such as the response-robot test bays captured in @fig-07-nist-test-arena, ensure repeatable benchmark comparisons by strictly constraining the test environment to known, fixed obstacle geometries.

::: {#fig-07-nist-test-arena fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Standardized robotic evaluation facility**: NIST response-robot test bays photographed in 2013 (Linda Joy/NIST); their test methods are standardized by ASTM subcommittee E54.09 on response robots. A zero-failure run across standardized bays establishes competence inside the arena and says nothing about glare, surface contaminants, or obstacles outside it." fig-alt="Photograph by Linda Joy/NIST of NIST response-robot test facility bays in 2013. Structured test spaces support repeatable trials within their fixture conditions."}
![](images/jpg/fig07_real_nist_test_arena.jpg){width="75%"}
:::

The standardized obstacle courses documented in @fig-07-nist-test-arena enable repeatable comparisons across robotic platforms under ASTM E54.09 test methods. However, their controlled geometry, uniform surface traction, and regulated indoor lighting also define the perimeter of empirical evidence. Validating system performance against factory chemical spills, erratic pedestrian crossings, or blinding solar glare requires intentionally introducing those environmental distributions into the test matrix.

These physical and statistical verification ceilings compel a fundamental architectural conclusion. Safety in physical AI cannot rest on statistical confidence derived from testing learned weights. The exposure that failure rates between $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-9}$ per hour demand, from `{python} ExposureWall.t_e6_math` to `{python} ExposureWall.t_e9_math` failure-free hours, shows that empirical test volume cannot serve as the primary safety argument. Deterministic runtime constraints must supply their own independent verification evidence, including explicit physical assumptions under which hazardous transitions are prevented and rigorous bounds on worst-case execution time. Empirical policy trials measure task competence and quantify intervention rates inside a nominal operational envelope; they do not prove that the system can contain arbitrary out-of-distribution failures. The burden of safety certification therefore shifts from the learned proposer to the deterministic permission path and verified physical safeguards, each of which must be evaluated through independent verification pathways.

A model-based stability certificate, such as the Lyapunov argument developed in @sec-appendix-control-lyapunov\index{Lyapunov function!stability certification}, provides structural guarantees that empirical finite trials cannot establish. When the learned proposer lacks a validated certificate for the declared plant and observation model, the embodied computing platform must provide architectural containment and targeted fault injection:

1. **Runtime Containment**: The system enforces hard physical bounds on the learned policy by delegating collaborative force thresholds, kinematic acceleration boundaries, and emergency stop triggers to an independent, deterministic permission path situated beneath the proposal boundary. The system's safety claims then rest on the permission path and its associated fallback strategies. These controllers rely on validated state estimation, conservative plant and actuator dynamics models, worst-case execution timing, and guaranteed stopping margins, all verified independently of the neural network proposer.
2. **Physical Fault Injection**: Rather than passively waiting for rare environmental disturbances or hardware faults to manifest during operational testing, systems engineers deliberately inject them on instrumented test benches. Because fault injection artificially alters the operational failure rate, these trials must be recorded in an isolated, explicitly labeled ledger rather than pooled with nominal operational draws.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The derivation of a fault list, by inverting design records and working forward from physical hazards, is developed in @sec-verification-deriving-fault-list.
:::

::: {#chk-eval-sample-size-mtbf .callout-checkpoint title="Sample size and MTBF evidence target"}

Before moving on, review sample size scaling and physical test limits:

- [ ] **Exposure-wall estimate**: Under a stationary Poisson failure model, estimate the failure-free hours a relaxed `{python} MtbfCampaign.mtbf_relaxed_str` MTBF target needs at 95 percent confidence, and determine whether one rig running continuously for a year could supply them.
- [ ] **Mechanical fatigue exhaustion**: Explain why a campaign's wheel revolutions cannot be compared with a bearing $\RatedFatigueLife$ rating without knowing the load the bearing carries.
- [ ] **Architectural containment vs. statistical sampling**: Explain why a task campaign needs separate evidence for runtime constraints and physical safeguards.

:::

Even under automated test cells and rigorous qualification protocols, statistical sampling of learned policies cannot demonstrate ultra-reliable autonomy. The integrity of an operational release decision depends on identifying precisely what remains unvisited by a finite test campaign and deploying verified runtime monitors to supervise those uncharacterized boundaries.

### Turning coverage gaps into runtime obligations

The fundamental limits of empirical evaluation originate directly in the closed-loop nature of embodied systems (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics). Because the physical states a machine traverses depend on the specific sequence of actuator commands admitted by the permission path, no static dataset can match the candidate policy's closed-loop state distribution. Physics simulators inevitably substitute an approximate transition model for the physical plant. A simulator that models warehouse floors as uniform, high-friction concrete cannot reveal how a mobile base behaves on a patch of spilled lubricant. Similarly, a simulation with idealized, instantaneous actuator torque cannot capture the phase lag introduced by an electric motor stator's electrical time constant\index{Actuator!stator delay}. Small physical discrepancies between simulated and real-world dynamics compound over closed-loop horizons, driving the physical platform into state regimes that never appeared in simulation. An empirical physical test bounds nothing beyond the specific closed-loop distribution it directly sampled.

The operational conclusion of the door campaign is correspondingly narrow. The physical trial records establish that a single software build deployed on a specific hardware platform (Unit 01), evaluated from the sampled initial poses under the specific ambient illumination and temperature present during testing, exhibited a per-cycle failure probability below `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.failure_upper_pct_str` at 95 percent confidence. This empirical record provides zero assurance regarding system behavior on a cold morning that thickens gearbox lubricant or derates actuator drive current\index{Hardware!thermal derating}, on an aging transmission whose compliance\index{Hardware!gearbox compliance} and backlash have increased through gear tooth wear, or against a door whose strike plate has shifted several millimeters out of true.

Testing across multiple physical units broadens the declared operating population, but executing additional runs solely on Unit 01 with a nominal strike plate merely tightens the binomial confidence interval (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds). Logging two thousand additional nominal cycles measures that single hardware unit with exquisite statistical precision while leaving displaced strike plates, payload variations, unit-to-unit manufacturing variations, and real-time bus jitter\index{Hardware!bus jitter} completely unsupported by empirical evidence.

Because finite evaluation cannot characterize behavior outside the sampled operational distribution, every unverified boundary of an empirical safety claim must be translated into an explicit runtime monitoring obligation. Each boundary requires an identifiable sensor signal, a calibrated detection threshold, a validated mitigation response, and deterministic enforcement by the permission path. Because operational distribution support is only partially observable and software out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors exhibit nonzero false-negative rates, environmental conditions that cannot be sensed with high confidence require hard ODD constraints, passive mechanical guards, or independent physical barriers.

The evaluation record captures these obligations in its `runtime_monitor_specs` field (@sec-evaluation-logs), across five mandatory monitoring channels whose detection coverage, latency, and mitigation responses must be independently validated:

1. **Input Support and Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!OOD detection} Quantifies whether incoming sensor observations remain within the support of the training and verification distributions using a calibrated score, with measured false-negative rates on held-out OOD test sets.
2. **Execution Latency and Freshness Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!execution latency} Tracks sensor observation age and neural inference execution time against separate hard deadlines. It verifies proposal renewal against nominal controller cadence (for example, verifying that the latch policy meets its `{python} EvalMachine.t_chunk_infer_str` p99 inference target inside its `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period at `{python} EvalMachine.chunk_rate_str`), logs deadline misses, and ensures that an expired chunk lease immediately engages a validated fallback. A p99 latency is an empirical percentile; it does not replace a hard real-time execution bound.
3. **Constraint Margin Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!constraint margin} Continuously tracks the distance between the current physical state and hardware protection boundaries, monitoring joint torque limits\index{Actuator!torque limit}, motor winding Joule heating\index{Actuator!Joule heating}, and physical obstacle clearances against calibrated stopping-distance models.
4. **Intervention Rate Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!intervention rate} Computes the running frequency of permission-path interventions and trajectory overrides as a warning of growing supervisory burden or behavioral drift. Preventive detection of a specified instability requires a declared window and threshold, with qualified detection-plus-response lead time. This warning does not replace instantaneous clearance and constraint checks or a feasible fallback.
5. **Environmental Assumption Monitor:**\index{Runtime monitoring!environmental assumptions} Verifies whether current physical conditions comply with operating design assumptions, tracking surface traction through wheel slip ratios and ambient illumination via calibrated photometric sensors.

A runtime monitor that merely records an anomaly to a diagnostic log provides zero physical protection. Under active control, if a newly generated policy proposal fails validation, the permission path rejects the replacement command without revoking the currently executing chunk, whose chunk lease is still valid. If the active command expires, encounters a safety violation, or lacks sufficient clearance, the permission path overrides the proposer and commands a validated fallback, such as a conservative speed restriction or a controlled deceleration to rest, provided that current state estimates, actuator torque headroom, and braking distances render that fallback physically feasible. Even when a neural policy produces timely, high-confidence proposals, every candidate control action ${\NominalControlCommand}_t$ must pass independent geometric clearance and actuator dynamic limits before the low-level hardware bridge applies torque to the plant.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The barrier condition that keeps braking feasible within the remaining clearance is developed in @sec-appendix-control-cbf.
:::

Certain catastrophic failure modes cannot be detected by any software runtime monitor. This vulnerability represents the **epistemic trap of software OOD monitors**: an algorithmic detector operates exclusively on digitized sensor telemetry and latent neural representations. When a physical transduction failure occurs, such as an immaculately clean architectural glass wall, a blinding specular laser reflection, or a camera occluded by uniform mud, the sensory telemetry itself is corrupted or absent. The perception pipeline may extract seemingly normal visual features from the reflection, reporting benign obstacle clearance while the physical chassis is on a collision course with the glass. Software cannot detect physical reality that hardware transduction failed to capture. In such failure modes, the proposal can satisfy every execution deadline, respect all motor torque envelopes, and exhibit familiar latent embedding vectors, yet drive the platform directly into an invisible obstacle. Physical safety against transduction failures cannot come from statistical evaluation or software-based OOD monitors. It requires architectural physical zoning\index{Safety!physical zoning}, hardware current limiters\index{Actuator!current limiters}, sensitive tactile bumpers, and physical safety barriers validated under explicit mechanical assumptions independently of the learned policy.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Observational indistinguishability, in which a hazardous state yields the same telemetry as a safe one until the response deadline, is developed in @sec-frontier-observational-indistinguishability-sub.
:::

These verification ceilings bind every evaluation campaign, no matter how rigorously executed. The empirical evidence preserved in an evaluation record is only as trustworthy as the measurement protocols that produced it. Procedural flaws, silent sensor drift, and statistical fallacies can corrupt an evaluation campaign long before its summary metrics reach the evaluation record.

## Empirical Evaluation Pitfalls and Metric Masking {#sec-evaluation-failure-modes}

Systematic errors undermining policy evaluation rarely stem from deliberate fraud. They arise when an evaluation protocol answers an easier question than the claim asks, creating statistical or procedural mirages that mask physical vulnerability.

### Six procedural evaluation pathologies {#sec-evaluation-procedural-pathologies}

Six recurring procedural flaws distort empirical evaluation: environment selection, metric drift, test-set contamination, optional stopping, denominator filtering, and substituting demonstrations for measurements.

**Pathology 1: Environment selection.** Environment selection occurs whenever the test bench is narrower than the claim. The twenty door runs all met the nominal strike plate at the `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` guarded approach with the base stopped and the tote rack empty. If the report states their success rate as the machine's ability to open the site's cage doors, the claim silently expands to the `{python} EvalMachine.n_absences_str` unsampled cells of the ledger and the loaded machine (@sec-evaluation-limits). Environment selection\index{Environment selection} is detected by comparing a condition ledger, which records the measured strike-plate position, approach speed, payload, and floor condition of every trial, against the boundaries of the claimed domain; a ledger that covers one cell establishes nothing about the others.

**Pathology 2: Metric drift and offline surrogate substitution.** Metric drift\index{Metric drift} occurs when the evaluation metric slides from physical closed-loop task completion toward an offline surrogate such as action agreement\index{Action agreement}, validation loss, action Mean Squared Error (MSE), or action cosine similarity against recorded expert buffers. Offline scoring is cheap, so the substitution happens gradually, and it inherits the ranking inversions of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics. Metric drift is prevented by keeping the primary evaluation metrics closed-loop physical observables, namely task-completion rate, ACR, MTBI, and $\InterventionDensity$. Protection violations, including unmitigated tripwire crossings, remain a separate recorded outcome and an explicit acceptance condition; they never justify dropping runs.

**Pathology 3: Unit-specific test set contamination.** Repeated tuning against a fixed evaluation setup creates unit-specific test set contamination\index{Test set contamination}. Adjusting the checkpoint or observation filtering after each batch on Unit 01 makes that robot and door part of development, not an independent holdout. The resulting improvement may depend on their particular backlash, calibration, and lighting. The countermeasure is to audit the history of policy versions, tuning decisions, and chassis identities, and to reserve fresh units and conditions for any claim that requires generalization beyond the development setup.

**Pathology 4: Optional stopping and multi-look inflation.** An engineer who watches a sequence of physical runs and halts as soon as the tally crosses a target reports a confidence the procedure does not have. Each look at the accumulating result is another chance for a false positive. `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_looks_str` independent 5 percent looks would have a `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_any_false_positive_pct_str` chance of at least one false positive. Repeated looks at one accumulating run are dependent, so the inflation for a real stopping rule must be computed for that rule. Optional stopping\index{Optional stopping} cannot be detected from summary tables or final pass rates. It is detected only by auditing the pre-registered trial protocol, verifying that sample sizes, stopping conditions, and evaluation milestones were fixed before the first physical run began. The calibrated alternative is a sequential rule declared in advance (@sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt).

**Pathology 5: Denominator filtering and the censored trial fallacy.** A related distortion occurs when the denominator is quietly filtered, breaking the full-denominator condition of @sec-evaluation-trial-protocol. A team that discards runs ending on timeouts, emergency stops, sensor communication drops, or permission-path overrides as invalid test artifacts reports success over the surviving trials only. Every metric of @sec-evaluation-what-measured then moves in the flattering direction: ACR rises, MTBI grows, intervention density falls toward zero, and the reset time spent clearing a jammed gripper disappears from the budget. If the arm opens the door on nine of ten attempts and the tenth needs an operator takeover to stop the gripper wedging against the latch, removing that attempt raises the apparent success rate from 90 percent to 100 percent and reports an infinite MTBI for the batch. Infrastructure aborts, such as dropped wireless packets, stalled kernel threads, or bus brownouts, also stay in the denominator. A base that stalls in the aisle because an operating system thread locked has failed its mission, whichever subsystem caused it, and removing such aborts evaluates an abstraction rather than the deployed machine. When physical constraints or safety limits truncate a run before its deadline $\CompletionDeadline$ expires, the trial stays in the ledger as not unassisted ($\UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = 0, {\TrialInterventionCount}_i \ge 1$), and for the unassisted-failure event it is right-censored rather than omitted. Reading survival on truncated trajectories as operational competence is the censored trial fallacy\index{Censored trial fallacy} of @sec-evaluation-evidence-regimes. Denominator filtering\index{Denominator filtering} is detected by cross-referencing low-level actuator telemetry and permission-path logs against the trial ledger, confirming that every power-on cycle, autonomy engagement, and physical reset corresponds to a recorded outcome.

::: {#ws-evaluation-nhtsa-40-percent-mirage .callout-war-story title="The 2017 NHTSA Autopilot crash rate mirage"}
**Context**: In January 2017, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) closed Preliminary Evaluation PE 16-007, which it had opened after a fatal Florida crash of a Model S operating in Autopilot mode [@nhtsa2017pe16007]. The closing report compared airbag-deployment crash rates in the subject Tesla vehicles before and after Autosteer was installed and stated that "the Tesla vehicles crash rate dropped by almost 40 percent after Autosteer installation," from 1.3 to 0.8 crashes per million miles.

**Mechanism**: The rate divided airbag deployments by miles driven before and after installation, and the report's own footnote noted that the rates "are for all miles travelled before and after Autopilot installation and are not limited to actual Autopilot use." The denominator therefore never measured exposure to Autosteer itself, and it was incomplete as well. A replication by Quality Control Systems Corporation found that the odometer reading at installation appears to have been reported for fewer than half of the vehicles, and that exact exposure before and after installation could be computed for only 13 percent of them [@qcs2019nhtsa]. The mileage NHTSA left uncounted, because it could be assigned to neither period, was concentrated among the vehicles with the least exposure before installation.

**Impact**: In the one cohort with complete exposure in both periods, the airbag-deployment crash rate rose 59 percent after installation, from 0.76 to 1.21 per million miles, a result the replication qualified with "if these data are to be believed." Its authors concluded that the overall 40 percent reduction was "an artifact of the Agency's treatment of mileage information that is actually missing in the underlying dataset." The replication does not measure Autosteer's effect either. It shows that the published denominator could not support the reported reduction.

**Response**: The correction came from outside the agency and two years after the closing report, because the per-vehicle mileage records that exposed the denominator were released only after a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Transportation [@qcs2019nhtsa].

**Systems lesson**: In physical AI evaluation, an unverified denominator produces a statistical mirage. Aggregating open-world mileage without engagement telemetry, operational design domain boundaries, and complete exposure records turns missing data into a safety claim. An evaluation audits the integrity of its denominator with the same rigor it applies to the failure events in its numerator.
:::

**Pathology 6: Substituting visual demonstrations for statistical measurements.** A successful video shows that the machine reached the goal under one sequence of conditions; without a sampling record, it does not establish how often that outcome recurs. Smooth $\SpecialEuclideanGroup$ kinematics (rigid-body motions in three dimensions)\index{SE(3) kinematics} can conceal small physical margins. A representative campaign needs predeclared sampling from the target ODD or separate per-stratum analysis, full-denominator accounting, and a sample size tied to its stated claim.

None of these pathologies is visible in the final pass rate. Each is caught only by auditing the record against the protocol that was declared before the first run, which is why the evaluation record keeps the protocol, the condition ledger, and the complete outcome sequence rather than the summary alone.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-evaluation-fallacies-pitfalls}

An empirical evaluation supports engineering claims only within the precise physical boundaries and statistical assumptions of its test protocol. In embodied machine learning systems, severe evaluation errors arise when teams extrapolate localized results across untested operational envelopes or attribute system-level safety guarantees to a learned policy when deterministic enforcement mechanisms actually did the work.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Repeated success in a single nominal condition proves broad operational readiness.*

Consider a door-opening evaluation campaign that repeats a single nominal configuration twenty times: a standard strike plate, an unencumbered approach vector, a stationary mobile base, and an empty payload rack. Under the binomial model\index{Evaluation!binomial model}, twenty flawless runs yield the `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` lower confidence bound derived in notebook \ref{nbk-evaluation-derivation-20-run-lower-bound} for that specific setup\index{Evaluation!confidence intervals}. However, they provide zero statistical evidence for the remaining cells of the operational ledger, such as misaligned latch hardware, floor irregularities, or a loaded tote rack that shifts the manipulator's center of mass and reduces actuator torque margins. Repeating identical trials merely sharpens precision on a single nominal operating point while leaving deployment-critical boundary conditions\index{Safety!operational envelope} completely unprobed. An engineering claim of operational readiness must explicitly define the target ODD, distribute test budgets across the physical parameters governing that domain, and bound uncertainty within each stratified cell. **Nominal repetition sharpens precision on a single cell; it provides zero evidence for the rest of the operational design domain.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Explicitly partition the declared operational design domain into a structured condition matrix, allocate trial quotas across all operational strata, and report confidence intervals per cell rather than pooling unstratified runs.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero failures in 1,000 trials proves compliance with a 99.9 percent reliability specification.*

Suppose a latch manipulation policy opens a door `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_fallacy_str` consecutive times without a single safety trip, evaluated against a specification requiring 99.9 percent success at 95 percent confidence. The observed sample success proportion is perfect ($\ObservedSuccessFraction = 1.00$). Standard Wald intervals based on the asymptotic Central Limit Theorem collapse into the degenerate point $[1.0, 1.0]$ because the estimated variance $\ObservedSuccessFraction(1-\ObservedSuccessFraction)/\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ vanishes identically at the boundary. However, an exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson inversion ($\SuccessLowerConfidenceLimit = 0.05^{1/\ZeroFailureTrialCount}$) demonstrates that the true one-sided lower confidence bound reaches only `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_fallacy_str`, falling decisively short of the 99.9 percent target (@tbl-07-confidence-bounds). Certifying compliance with that target requires `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_999_str` consecutive clean runs. A parallel fallacy recurs in early-stage pilot testing: observing zero failures across 20 trials ($\SuccessLowerConfidenceLimit =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str`) cannot demonstrate even a modest 90 percent success bound (`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_90_str` clean runs required), much less an industrial 99 percent standard (`{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_req_99_str` clean runs required). Test budgets must be derived directly from the required confidence level and reliability target before execution begins, and validation reports must document exact non-asymptotic bounds rather than empirical success ratios. **Zero failures across an insufficient sample size represent an evidence deficit, not empirical proof of compliance.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Reject asymptotic Wald intervals near parameter boundaries. Precalculate the minimum sample budget using the exact non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson formulation ($\ZeroFailureTrialCount = \lceil \ln\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel / \ln \TargetTrialSuccessProbability \rceil$) or its continuous-time counterpart for exposure hours ($\FailureObservationInterval \ge 3.0/\ConstantHazardRate$), and report exact one-sided lower confidence bounds in all compliance audits.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *High offline action agreement on static logs guarantees closed-loop physical stability.*

An evaluation report citing close agreement with expert actions\index{Evaluation!action agreement} on recorded teleoperation logs, whether framed as negligible action mean squared error (MSE), high discrete token prediction accuracy, low validation perplexity, or high action cosine similarity, measures dataset imitation on static buffers and nothing more. As demonstrated by the mobile aisle policy in @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics, a policy can match its offline demonstrations with near-zero error and still exhaust its lateral clearance through the kinematic integration of a minute, persistent heading bias. Compounding this error, covariate shift\index{Evaluation!covariate shift} drives the system into unmodeled state spaces once trajectory drift departs from the demonstration support.

Physical contact introduces even sharper failure modes. At non-Lipschitz mechanical interfaces, sub-millimeter positional deviations that barely register in aggregate MSE trigger destructive reaction forces ($\ContactReactionForce = \ContactStiffness \FiniteChange \ContactPointPosition$) and mechanical wedging. This produces dramatic ranking inversions where policies with lower offline MSE fail completely while policies with higher MSE succeed. Directional metrics such as cosine similarity fail for complementary reasons: they ignore command magnitude entirely. A policy commanding the correct directional vector with 25 percent too little force stalls below a latch's breakout threshold, whereas commanding 150 percent of the required force can trip protective torque boundaries. Offline metrics serve well as initial screening filters to discard defective training checkpoints, but empirical closed-loop capability must be evaluated using physical observables, namely task-completion rate, ACR, MTBI, and $\InterventionDensity$, tracked against the complete execution denominator, with protection outcomes recorded separately. Even then, these finite-sample empirical metrics do not constitute a formal proof of closed-loop stability\index{Control!closed-loop stability}. **Offline validation loss, MSE, and cosine similarity measure dataset mimicry; closed-loop physical dynamics decide survival.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Treat offline loss, action MSE, and cosine similarity strictly as preliminary triage filters. Require closed-loop physical rollouts with full-denominator accounting to support behavioral claims, and require separate model-based Lyapunov or invariant set analyses for any formal stability guarantee.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Peeking at accumulating rollouts and terminating testing early inflates false safety certification.*

When an engineering team halts an evaluation campaign after 30 consecutive clean runs simply because intermediate results look favorable, and then reports the confidence bounds of a fixed-sample protocol, they commit sequential peeking. Halting on a winning streak distorts the underlying statistical distribution; an adaptive stopping rule inflates the false-positive rate, rendering standard fixed-sample confidence calculations invalid. While a predeclared zero-failure test can terminate upon the first observed failure to reject an inadequate policy, terminating early to accept a candidate requires an explicit sequential design. Sequential probability ratio testing provides a mathematically sound alternative: Ville's martingale inequality bounds the probability of false acceptance by $e^{-\SprtUpperBoundary}$ for any declared acceptance threshold $\SprtUpperBoundary$, which resolves to $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel/(1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate)$ under classic Wald boundaries (@sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt). **Choose the stopping rule before collecting outcomes, and report the error guarantee for that rule.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Pre-register sequential decision boundaries ($\SprtUpperBoundary \approx \ln((1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate)/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel)$, $\SprtLowerBoundary \approx \ln(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate/(1-\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel))$) before running trials. Update the cumulative log-likelihood ratio $\SequentialLogLikelihoodRatio$ after each physical rollout, and award the declared SPRT acceptance or rejection decision only when the statistic crosses its corresponding threshold. A physical hazard or invalidating protocol evidence can terminate the campaign independently. Preserve the complete ledger and termination reason without awarding favorable inferential status unsupported by the declared statistical rule.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Crediting the learned policy with surviving transport stalls that the enforcement architecture handled.*

Suppose a mobile manipulator completes 50 nominal aisle navigation trials, leading the engineering team to credit the learned transformer policy with inherent robustness against serializer/deserializer (SerDes) bus jitter\index{Hardware!SerDes jitter}. Later, a qualification trial injects a synthetic mailbox stall that exceeds the `{python} EvalMachine.t_lease_str` chunk lease. The lease\index{Chunk lease!expiry under a stall} expires, prompting the deterministic permission path to detect the deadline miss and command an immediate controlled dynamic stop, analogous to an industrial Category 1 stop\index{Safety!Category 1 stop} (a controlled deceleration under drive power, with torque removed once the machine stands still), as classified in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories. This safe recovery is executed entirely by the enforcement architecture, not the learned model. Nominal task completion does not prove that the neural network weights can detect, absorb, or recover from communication dropouts. Rigorous fault injection\index{Evaluation!fault injection} must evaluate the permission path's detection latency and stopping distance margins under stress, and the final evaluation report must attribute safety enforcement directly to the hardware and runtime mechanisms that actually executed the stop. **Do not credit unverified neural weights with safety guarantees provided by the deterministic permission path.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Conduct systematic fault injection, including synthetic communication stalls and sensor frame drops, to independently benchmark the permission path's braking envelope, and attribute safety mechanisms strictly to the hardware and software layers that executed them.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Zero physical collisions or hardware damage in testing proves high autonomous policy reliability.*

When an autonomous vehicle or mobile manipulator completes an extended test campaign without collisions, teams frequently declare that the policy demonstrated exceptional reliability (for example, claiming an MTBF equal to the total logged run time). However, if human safety operators disengaged the autonomy system or the permission path intervened repeatedly to avert impending collisions, the zero-damage outcome ($\DamageEventCount = 0$) occurred only because the protective safety envelope actively censored catastrophic trajectories. What the testbed truly recorded was a sequence of intervention events. True autonomous capability must be evaluated through ACR and MTBI. Frequent human takeovers render commercial deployments economically unviable, whereas small automatic clips by the permission path may represent routine boundary regulation; an evaluation report must classify and audit these intervention tiers separately. Censoring interventions or tallying assisted rollouts as unassisted policy successes confuses the protective competence of the supervisory envelope with the autonomous competence of the learned policy. **Zero collisions under active safety supervision must be interpreted alongside interventions; they do not by themselves establish policy reliability or complete protection coverage.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Enforce strict full-denominator accounting. Record every human takeover, permission-path clamping action, and virtual tripwire breach as an autonomy disengagement ($\UnassistedSuccessIndicator_i = 0, {\TrialInterventionCount}_i \ge 1$). Report these unassisted autonomy metrics alongside overall task completion rates, mission cycle times, and protective safety statistics.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Qualifying a policy on a single reference robot assumes zero unit-to-unit hardware variance across the fleet.*

Consider an engineering team that logs 300 failure-free trials on a single laboratory robot (Unit 01) and certifies the policy for fleet deployment. When deployed onto Unit 02 on the manufacturing floor, the identical policy repeatedly jams against fixtures or exhibits severe actuator chatter. As detailed in @sec-evaluation-what-measured, physical unit-to-unit variations (transmission lost motion, harmonic drive compliance and stiffness, structural link flexure under load, camera mounting misalignments, and motor winding tolerances) substantially alter the plant transfer function across robot builds. Qualifying a policy on a single "golden unit" merely calibrates the model to that individual chassis's electromechanical profile rather than establishing fleet-wide reliability. Furthermore, running evaluations during a single shift overlooks non-stationary environmental factors: diurnal sunlight glare sweeping across vision sensors, floor traction changes driven by ambient humidity, or thermal drift from motor winding resistance heating ($\WindingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance$) that alter plant dynamics without altering a single neural network parameter. **Evaluating a single robot chassis characterizes that specific unit's mechanical quirks; fleet release requires stratifying trials across the manufacturing distribution.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Stratify physical qualification protocols across multiple chassis serial numbers sampled from the fleet manufacturing distribution $\FleetManufacturingDistribution$. Audit unit-specific lost motion and kinematic link offsets prior to evaluation, and reserve final acceptance testing for untouched production units that were never used during policy development or hyperparameter tuning.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Hardware divergence among nominally identical robots in a fleet is established in @sec-data-fleet-divergence.
:::

## Summary {#sec-evaluation-summary}

Closed-loop evaluation characterizes the fully coupled execution system: the proposer policy, the permission path, the physical plant, the surrounding environment, and the experimental protocol. Consequently, an empirical success rate never describes a static weight checkpoint in isolation; it characterizes a declared population of operational trajectories. Because the machine's admitted actions dictate the future states it encounters, which is the second law, endogenous data, applied to testing, only closed-loop execution through the active permission path reveals how the proposer truly behaves. Open-loop evaluations on pre-recorded datasets remain blind to the cascading compounding errors that real-world interaction induces.

A zero-failure confidence bound quantifies performance over this sampled population under explicit sampling assumptions. When safety tripwires intervene to prevent physical damage, they censor trials right at the operational safety boundary, keeping empirical testing confined to the envelope the experimental campaign can safely explore. Gathering additional trials narrows statistical uncertainty within that sampled distribution, but it cannot expand the boundaries of the characterized population. Furthermore, the physical exposure wall imposes a fundamental ceiling: validating ultra-rare hazard rates requires far more continuous operating hours than any single physical platform can feasibly run.

The robotic door-opening campaign illustrates the precise scope of an empirical engineering claim. Twenty incident-free trials establish a statistical lower bound on success at the nominal strike plate and the guarded approach speed, with the base stopped and the tote rack empty. That evidence justifies no claims about displaced strike plates omitted from the demonstration dataset, nor does it guarantee performance when carrying heavy payloads. To handle these uncharacterized regimes safely, the engineering team maintains a coverage gap catalog that explicitly documents every unvisited condition. Rather than trusting an unverified proposer policy or relying on an out-of-distribution detector that can fail when encountering novel inputs, the system delegates safety in these unvisited regions to independent physical constraints and verified fallback behaviors in the permission path.

The stipulated recovery branch demonstrates how engineers systematically expand this operational boundary over time. When developers gather targeted experience to train an updated candidate policy, they must validate it through independent regression testing on nominal regimes alongside rigorous qualification on displaced plates. An initial evaluation archive never represents a permanent barrier to capability; rather, it establishes an empirical baseline from which verified competence can methodically advance.

The ultimate output of a closed-loop testing campaign is the evaluation record. Four core artifacts from this record govern downstream deployment and system safety:

1. *Bounded operational claim:* The target ODD\index{Operational design domain!target ODD}, established within the broader declared ODD of the policy manifest, specifying the precise environmental and kinematic envelope where closed-loop performance has been empirically characterized.
2. *Reproducible configuration and ledger:* Cryptographic digests of neural network weights, controller firmware, and sensor calibrations, paired with measured hardware tolerances and an unedited trial ledger. Retaining every attempted, aborted, and overridden trial in the denominator is essential to compute honest task-completion, autonomy, intervention, and reset metrics ($\text{ACR}$, MTBI, $\InterventionDensity$, $\ResetLatency$), with protection outcomes recorded separately.
3. *Coverage gap catalog:* A systematic audit detailing known data omissions from training demonstrations, operational regimes unvisited during testing, and specific hardware units that remain uncharacterized.
4. *Runtime monitor specifications:* Explicit signal definitions, trigger thresholds, and tested fallback maneuvers that the permission path must execute whenever an observable safety boundary is reached\index{Runtime monitoring}.

@Tbl-07-key-equations summarizes the foundational mathematical relationships that support these operational decisions, linking each formal bound to its engineering consequence.

| Equation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                       | Derived in                                     |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|
| $\TrialSuccessProbability(\OperationalTestDistribution) = \mathbb{E}_{\TrialCondition \sim \OperationalTestDistribution}[\EvaluationPredicate(\text{Traj}(\TrialCondition))]$                                                                      | The estimand: a success rate belongs to the declared population $\OperationalTestDistribution$, not to the weights              | @eq-eval-estimand                              |
| $\DriftImpactTime = \LateralClearance/(\BaseForwardSpeed \sin \FiniteChange\HeadingAngle)$                                                                                                                                                         | How soon a persistent heading bias spends clearance that open-loop scoring never sees                                           | @eq-eval-clearance-time                        |
| $\SuccessLowerConfidenceLimit = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel^{1/\ZeroFailureTrialCount}$                                                                                                                                                       | Success lower limit after $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ clean trials                                                                 | @eq-eval-zero-failure-bound                    |
| $\FailureUpperConfidenceLimit \approx 3/\ZeroFailureTrialCount$                                                                                                                                                                                    | Rule of three: failure upper limit at 95% confidence, and $\ZeroFailureTrialCount \approx 3/(1-\TargetTrialSuccessProbability)$ | @eq-eval-rule-of-three                         |
| $\ZeroFailureTrialCount = \lceil \ln \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel / \ln \TargetTrialSuccessProbability \rceil$                                                                                                                                 | Clean trials a claim needs; each added nine costs ten times the trials                                                          | @eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size              |
| $\Pr(\BinomialSuccessCount \ge \SuccessfulTrialCount \mid \TrialCount, \TrialSuccessProbability) = \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$                                                                                                               | Success lower limit when the record contains failures                                                                           | @eq-eval-bound-with-failures                   |
| $\SequentialLogLikelihoodRatio$ against $\SprtUpperBoundary \approx \ln((1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate)/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel)$, $\SprtLowerBoundary \approx \ln(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate/(1-\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel))$ | Sequential acceptance or rejection with both error rates declared before the first run                                          | @eq-eval-sprt-llr and @eq-eval-sprt-boundaries |
| $\FailureObservationInterval \ge \ln(1/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel)/\ConstantHazardRate$                                                                                                                                                      | Exposure wall: failure-free hours before a hazard rate can be bounded                                                           | @eq-eval-exposure-wall                         |
