: **Key equations of closed-loop evaluation**: Each equation fixes one quantity a campaign must declare or report. The statistical bounds assume independent, identically distributed draws from the declared population; the kinematic and contact relations are first-order models whose inputs must be measured on the machine. {#tbl-07-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,42,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Closed-loop evaluation and reliability"}
* **A success rate belongs to a population**: Any empirical success metric reflects the coupled proposer policy, permission path, physical plant, environment, and trial protocol. Additional trials narrow uncertainty within sampled conditions, but evaluating new hardware units or altered operating regimes requires fresh empirical evidence.
* **Select evaluation regimes to match engineering questions**: Offline replay validates predictive accuracy and compute budgets, simulation tests closed-loop feedback under modeled dynamics, shadow deployment tests runtime execution against live sensor streams, and constrained physical trials expose real unmodeled contact. Each evaluation modality leaves distinct coverage gaps; their results cannot be pooled as interchangeable evidence.
* **Separate task completion from protective interventions**: Autonomous completion rate ($\text{ACR}$) quantifies unassisted task success, whereas mean time between interventions (MTBI) and intervention density characterize the operational burden of specific safety tripwires. Physical task success and protective safety outcomes must be tracked independently. In addition, reset latency ($\ResetLatency$) captures the operational overhead of recovering after a safety disengagement. Recording every attempted run prevents safety supervision from artificially inflating policy performance.
* **Failure-free trials leave residual statistical uncertainty**: Twenty consecutive successful trials yield a one-sided 95 percent success lower bound of `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_pct_str` under independent and identically distributed sampling. Reliability targets and statistical confidence levels dictate the required trial budget. Predeclared, calibrated sequential testing rules allow early stopping decisions without introducing post hoc selection bias.
* **Rare hazards demand independent physical safeguards**: Physical testing campaigns cannot feasibly supply the millions of failure-free operating hours required to bound catastrophic risk. Runtime monitors, mechanical interlocks, and physical safety boundaries require independent validation of their sensing fidelity, actuation latency, and fallback dynamics; a high policy success rate can never substitute for verified protective mechanisms.
* **The evaluation record binds capability to operational limits**: The record documents what the proposer achieved within its target ODD, preserves an unedited trial ledger, and highlights unsupported operational conditions. Its monitor specifications guide runtime safety design, while unmonitorable coverage gaps impose firm operational restrictions on deployment claims.
:::

The second law, endogenous data, closes Part II by leaving every evaluation record conditional on the closed loop that produced it. A sequence of incident-free trials samples only the trajectory distribution generated by admitted actions; it neither explores every physically reachable state nor certifies the absence of hazards outside the tested envelope. Systems engineers must carry both the characterized competence and the uncharacterized uncertainty forward into runtime system design. The evaluation record formalizes this transition through its target operational design domain, coverage gap catalog, and monitoring requirements. With the evaluation record, the first of the record chain's two strands is complete, pairing the plant limits of the limit record with the bounded competence recorded here. Part III builds the second strand, the live observations and proposals that meet the first at the permission decision on every control tick.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-evaluation-history}

The statistical foundations of closed-loop evaluation were established long before autonomous systems encountered physical hardware. Standard textbook treatments of binomial confidence intervals rely on asymptotic normality, yet normal approximations fail catastrophically near the extreme boundaries ($\TrialSuccessProbability \approx 0$ or $\TrialSuccessProbability \approx 1$) where robot qualification and safety certification operate. @wilson1927probable resolved the degeneracy of the textbook interval at zero failures by inverting the score test, ensuring that confidence intervals would not collapse to zero width on a spotless empirical record. @clopper1934use went further by directly inverting the cumulative binomial distribution to produce the exact, conservative confidence bounds that modern physical qualification audits require. In clinical trials evaluating rare adverse medical events, @hanley1983nothing popularized the "rule of three" as an accessible analytical shorthand for zero-failure campaigns, establishing that when zero incidents occur across $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ independent trials, an upper 95 percent confidence bound on the true event probability is approximately $3/\ZeroFailureTrialCount$. Decades later, @brown2001interval demonstrated the persistent systematic flaws and erratic coverage probability of standard Wald intervals, demonstrating why rigorous evaluation campaigns for embodied agents must rely on exact binomial methods or inverted score statistics rather than asymptotic Gaussian assumptions.

The formal methodology for designing controlled evaluation campaigns emerged from agricultural experimentation and industrial manufacturing. @fisher1935design formulated the core principles of randomized design, Latin squares, and blocking to prevent uncontrolled environmental factors, such as thermal drift, surface wear, and ambient lighting shifts, from being mistaken for genuine differences in algorithmic performance. Fisher's exact test for contingency tables [@fisher1922interpretation] remains the standard baseline when comparing categorical success rates between discrete policy checkpoints under small sample sizes. During the Second World War, the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University introduced sequential hypothesis testing to inspect manufacturing lots efficiently without sacrificing statistical rigor; @wald1945sequential published this Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) once military classification was lifted. The underlying mathematical machinery that guarantees valid stopping times and bounds Type I and Type II errors traces back to the martingale formulation of @ville1939etude. In contemporary robot learning, these martingale arguments directly underwrite sequential testing protocols and anytime-valid confidence sequences, enabling practitioners to evaluate candidate policies adaptively and terminate underperforming runs early without invalidating target significance guarantees [@snyder2025policy].

The physical impossibility of validating safety-critical systems purely through black-box testing, the exposure wall, became evident during the development of fly-by-wire avionics. @butler1993infeasibility demonstrated that verifying catastrophic failure rates on the order of $10^{-9}$ per flight hour requires operational test durations spanning hundreds of thousands of years, proving that ultra-high reliability cannot be certified through black-box testing alone and must instead rely on formal architecture, modular containment, and provable safety envelopes. @kalra2016rr1478 applied this statistical reality to autonomous road vehicles, demonstrating that establishing statistical proof of safety parity with human drivers requires driving hundreds of millions or billions of physical miles across complex operational domains. Within machine learning, the gap between offline accuracy and online execution stems from the fundamental dynamics of closed loops. When @pomerleau1989alvinn demonstrated autonomous steering via artificial neural networks, small prediction errors caused the vehicle to drift into unfamiliar road configurations that were absent from the human demonstration dataset. @ross2010efficient and @ross2011reduction formalized this breakdown by showing that distribution shift in sequential decision problems causes one-step prediction errors to compound quadratically over the planning horizon, producing a rigorous bound on the gap between open-loop validation and closed-loop rollouts. A defensible evaluation campaign brings these disciplines together: it delineates the operational design domain, accounts for human interventions as primary events within the statistical denominator, and confines the policy to verified envelopes when environmental conditions exceed tested bounds.

For further reading, six foundational works trace the trajectory from small-sample statistical theory to modern closed-loop robot evaluation:

- @brown2001interval provides a definitive comparative analysis of binomial confidence intervals, exposing the systematic under-coverage of asymptotic approximations and motivating the exact bounds detailed in @sec-evaluation-bounds-with-failures.
- @wald1945sequential formulates the Sequential Probability Ratio Test, establishing the mathematical boundaries and error guarantees applied to checkpoint screening in @sec-evaluation-sequential-sprt.
- @butler1993infeasibility delivers a foundational proof that operational testing alone cannot certify ultra-high reliability in critical software systems, explaining why physical certification must lean on architectural safety design.
- @kalra2016rr1478 quantifies the exposure wall for autonomous driving, providing accessible mathematical models and tables that show the hundreds of millions to billions of miles needed to measure catastrophic failure rates empirically.
- @ross2011reduction provides the theoretical analysis of compounding error under policy-induced distribution shift and introduces Dataset Aggregation (DAgger), formalizing why offline validation metrics fail to predict closed-loop performance.
- @kressgazit2024robot establishes concrete reporting standards and metrology guidelines for physical robot evaluation, offering operational checklists covering trial counts, initial state distributions, blind evaluations, and failure mode accounting.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From evaluation records to perception"}
Part II ends with a record that confines trust in the learned proposer to its target ODD and names the runtime monitors the rest of the machine must supply. Part III builds the runtime that meets those obligations. The first of them falls on perception, because an input-support monitor or a latency monitor can act only on observations that carry their capture time, their coordinate frame, and their uncertainty. @Sec-perception opens on a detection that is correct and already late, because the base keeps moving while the camera exposes, reads out, and infers, and it follows that measurement from the sensor to a spatial claim that the permission path can date, place, and bound before it permits motion.
:::
